ANNOUNCEMENT OF VOLUNTARY CONTRIBUTIONS TO OVERCOME FINANCIAL DIFFICULTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Members of the House will be aware that in spite of the efforts of the United Nations special committee on peace keeping operations, no agreement has been reached at the United Nations on methods to discharge the accumulated financial obligations occasioned by the refusal of some member states to pay their assessments for the United Nations Emergency Force and the United Nations operation in the Congo. The total debt is something over $100 million.
In the hope that by constructive action the present deadlock might be broken, a number of governments are today announcing pledges of voluntary and unconditional contributions to help the United Nations out of its present financial difficulties, and they have so informed the Secretary General of the United Nations. The Canadian Government has participated in the consultations which led to this action, and I now wish to associate Canada with it. The Government has decided, subject to approval by Parliament, to make a similar pledge in the amount of $4 million. I have instructed our permanent representative to the United Nations to convey this decision to the Secretary General, and he will be doing so at 3.30 this afternoon. I also hope to see the Secretary General later today or tomorrow to discuss this and other matters.
The Canadian Government's pledge is made without prejudice to our support for the policy of collective financial responsibility for duly authorized peace keeping operations. Our understanding is that this pledge will form part of any formal agreement for contributions to relieve the organization's indebtedness if and when such agreement is reached. I do not exclude the possibility that at a later stage it may become necessary for us to supplement this pledge.
I should like to make it clear that in coming to this decision the governments associated
with this initiative have not underestimated the serious differences which have thus far defied solution. But we believe that rather than let the United Nations founder on this issue of principle, the time has come for as many states as possible to make a joint effort to restore the solvency of the United Nations, to create conditions which will make it possible for the assembly to meet normally next September, and to preserve the capacity of the United Nations to continue to perform its essential functioning in the maintenance of international peace and security.
The group of member states which have joined in this initiative today have traditionally been in the forefront of those which have come to the aid of the United Nations in times of stress. Obviously we cannot, of ourselves, solve the problem. But we can give a lead, and this we have done in the hope and expectation that the action of these nations will persuade others to follow suit so that the United Nations will be restored to solvency by the time the next general assembly reconvenes in September.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure every Member shares the concern of the Government over the crisis that has been facing the United Nations throughout these past months. The announcement that has been made is, of course, one to which we give our complete support at this time.
I think there are two questions that arise in our minds in considering this issue. The first is that we are inclined to question the sincerity of those nations which are failing to measure up to their responsibilities in regard to the United Nations peace keeping operations. The other question is just how long the United Nations can continue to function and be sustained in this fashion. There is no doubt that the time will come, perhaps very soon, when definite decisions will have to be made and positive steps taken to assure the United Nations of adequate support in carrying out its responsibilities.
As has been pointed out, Mr. Speaker, Canada is already carrying a very heavy responsibility with regard to peace keeping operations, recognizing that this is the one area in which we can make our greatest contribution. Reference has been made to the fact that Canada is already paying the full cost of maintaining its contingent in Cyprus as well as fulfilling its responsibilities in other fields.
As I have said, while we support every effort to maintain peace and security in the world and are prepared to make an adequate contribution for that purpose, we trust the time will come very soon when those other nations which have precipitated this situation will recognize and accept their responsibilities as well.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DORION COMMISSION-ALLEGED LEAK OF CONTENTS OF REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of stories have appeared in newspapers over the week end with respect to an alleged leak of the report of the Dorion inquiry. I wish to emphasize, as the Prime Minister said in London, that the Government is in no position to know whether there has been a leak since no member of the Government is aware of the contents of the report.
When these newspaper stories appeared I thought it my duty to get in touch with Chief Justice Dorion, who has full and sole responsibility for the preparation of the report and its transmission to the Government. I instructed the Privy Council office, which is responsible for liaison with Chief Justice Dorion, to get in touch with him yesterday. Mr. Chief Justice Dorion said he wished to reflect about this whole matter, and that he would call me on Monday.
This morning I received a telephone call from the Chief Justice, who has authorized me to inform the House of the following statement which he has given to the press. Since he read it to me in French I would prefer to use the text as given to me by the Chief Justice.

I was extremely surprised to learn that Southam News Services took the liberty of publishing what purports to be parts of my report. For the completion of this report, I had of course to rely on the co-operation of some federal civil servants. When I left Ottawa on June 10, I had completed the writing of the report. I then asked Mr. Andre Desjardins, a lawyer with the Commission, to look after the final draft, the translation and the printing of the report. Mr. Desjardins had three copies
June 21, 1965

Administration of Justice made, one for himself and the two others to be handed over, by sections, to the translators under Mr. M. H. Mayer whom I had met before leaving Ottawa and in whom X have full and complete confidence.
According to the press report, this news agency allegedly obtained its information from a source which is, according to the agency, usually reliable in such matters. If such is the case, I do not believe it should be too difficult to identify that source. The federal government certainly has the means to conduct the investigations required in order to exercise whatever recourse is necessary.

That is the end of the statement as given to me by the Chief Justice. In our conversation the Chief Justice emphasized what is apparent in the statement I have just quoted. He is not expressing any opinion on whether or not there has been a leak. None of us can have even a preliminary view on this until we know what is in the report.
Nevertheless, given the reports which appeared in the papers I also asked Chief Justice Dorion whether he would undertake an investigation with respect to the security of the arrangements for preparing the report. The Chief Justice did not wish to do so, and expressed the view that any formal inquiry would be inappropriate, at this stage at least.
We agreed, however, that a preliminary examination of the facts relating to the security of the arrangements could be undertaken. I have accordingly asked the R.C.M. Police to carry out a preliminary investigation of this kind in close co-operation with Chief Justice Dorion.
Because of the speculation which now surrounds this report, the Prime Minister has indicated that in his view it should be transmitted to the Government at the earliest possible date. I conveyed this view to Chief Justice Dorion today. He informed me the work is already being done on the tightest practicable schedule, and he doubts whether it would be possible to have the report available for transmission to the Government before the end of the week.
I can, of course, assure the House that as soon as the report is received by the Government it will be tabled in Parliament.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT. DUTIES, ETC.
PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT. DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that many, and I hope all, hon. Members have carefully considered this resolution. Its purpose, as indicated in the resolution itself, is to establish an Indian Claims Commission to consider fully the claims of Indian bands against the Crown.
The establishment of such a Commission has been advocated for many years, not only by Indians but by many others, in order that a tribunal might be set up which could effectively deal with claims put forward by the Indians of Canada. The claims made may or may not have legitimate bases; some of them undoubtedly have, but it is felt that when so many of these claims are being put forward, whether rightly or wrongly, there should be a tribunal set up to determine them, and settle them once and for all.
I think most people who have studied this problem, and more particularly those with any training in the law, will appreciate that it is impossible to have these claims dealt with in the law courts, where strict rules of evidence must be followed and where other legal technicalities would have to be adhered to. These claims, I might say, have mainly to do with allegations that lands were taken without proper compensation agreed upon by treaty or otherwise; also they involve failure to discharge treaty obligations, improper use of Indian trust funds, and in general include claims based on the alleged failure of Canada to deal in a fair and equitable manner with our native people, the Indians.
Two joint committees of the Senate and House of Commons which examined Indian affairs in the years 1946 to 1948 and again in 1959 to 1961, after hearing the evidence of Indians and others, recommended that a Claims Commission be established to hear and settle in an equitable manner these claims. I might say that from my perusal of Hansard and discussions I have had with officials of my Department, I believe and I am advised that the establishment of such an Indian Claims Commission has received general suport in the past from members of all parties in the Commons, and the Indians generally have come to expect that such a Commission would be established.
In the United States, after many years of advocacy, an Indian Claims Commission was established in 1946. This Commission was given very broad terms of reference to

deal with claims of Indian tribes, which are similar in many respects to those raised by the Indian bands and tribes in Canada. Indians in Canada are very well aware of the work of this Commission in the United States and they have continued-not only Indians but others who are interested in the subject-to press for a comparable tribunal in Canada to deal with these claims. I might say, Mr. Chairman-and I have had some experience myself-that some Indians feel such a Commission would be just another device concocted by the whites to whittle away Indian rights. We must do our best not only to establish this Commission as soon as possible, but when it is set up we must do what we can to ensure that everything is done to correct and remove any such impression.
Hon. Members will recall that in December, 1963 Bill No. C-130 was introduced in this House to establish such a Claims Commission. Immediately thereafter copies of the Bill were distributed to Indian organizations, Indian bands and other interested groups and individuals in all parts of Canada for study. The Bill now proposed and covered by the resolution before the Committee is similar in objectives but differs in some major respects, in that it includes several suggestions that were made by the Indian bands and others since the bill of December, 1963 was introduced.
The need to settle the claims of our native people, the Indians, is just as great today as it was when the earlier resolution was approved by a Committee of this House in December, 1963. The mere existence of these claims is an impediment, I believe, to progress. Some of the claims have their roots in the very deep past; they go back well over 100 years. Others are of more recent origin. But whether ancient or new, or whatever the merits of the claims may be, it is apparent that there is a continuing sense of grievance among the Indians concerned; they have felt that action should have been taken long ago, and that it is time for us to take action which will permit their claims to be dealt with in justice and fairness.
I firmly believe, therefore-and here I speak strongly on behalf of the Government-that it is highly desirable at this time to provide a means whereby the Indians can state their claims fully and have them determined. We hope that, once we have done so, these old controversies will be laid at rest, and by so doing will go a long way toward building the kind of confidence in the intentions of Parliament and the intentions of the Canadian
June 21, 1965

people which is so necessary for the future development of the Indian population of this country.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
As I have already advised the Committee, it is the Government's intention to recommend that this bill be referred to a Committee for detailed consideration. In view of the great interest taken by Members of the other place and the fact that they have participated in two joint Committees which recommended that such a Commission be appointed, we intend to propose that the bill be studied by a Joint Committee of the two Houses of Parliament. When this bill is before the Joint Committee, and whenever it is considered necessary or desirable for me to do so, I, with the assistance of the officials of my Department in the Indian Affairs Branch, will deal with the various representations which were made to us during the year 1964 and early this year with respect to the former claims bill.
At this stage I will content myself by drawing attention to the objectives of the bill as outlined in the resolution. If all hon. Members have read it I need not take much of their time, but briefly they call for a measure to provide for the establishment of an Indian Claims Commission; to outline the duties of the Commission, its decisions and awards; to provide for appeals from the decisions and awards of the Commission to an Indian Claims appeal court; to provide assistance to Indian bands in preparing and pursuing claims-I might say that was one of the matters recommended in several of the briefs that we received-and finally, to enact such financial provisions as may be necessary to accomplish the purposes of the Act.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT. DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we on this side, and I am sure all hon. Members of the Opposition, welcome this very long delayed and much needed resolution which precedes the bill establishing the Indian Claims Commission. This afternoon we heard the Acting Prime Minister indicate that the Government intended to take certain steps with regard to helping make up a deficit on the part of the United Nations.
This, of course, underlines the fact that Canada plays a very considerable part in connection with peace keeping operations around the world, and in addition, of course, through the Colombo Plan and other measures has participated very substantially in assisting underdeveloped nations. But I want to emphasize that for my part I think until

Indian Claims Commission we have remedied the problem we have in our own country by legislation of this kind and by other measures, our opportunities to participate in this very worth-while work throughout the world must be somewhat lessened.
I welcome the announcement by the Minister that another joint committee will be set up. I had the privilege of serving on the last joint committee, and our labours extended over a period of three years. A number of witnesses were called and there was an extensive examination-

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT. DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will permit an interjection at this point, I hope that the passage of this legislation will not take even three months, let alone three years.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT. DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I hope so too; because it was in 1961 that the report was made, and it is now 1965. So the three years of discussion and the four years intervening between the filing of the report and introduction of the legislation makes a very long period of gestation.
I also wanted to refer to what the Minister said regarding the situation in this country in the past, particularly vis-a-vis the United States. In the United States for a great many years-hon. Members may not be aware of this-such treaties were given the same solemn obligation as were international treaties between sovereign countries. I think that was the case until about 1870 or 1880. This accordingly lent to treaties signed by the national government of the United States and the Indian people a far greater measure of solemnity, and gave them far greater opportunities to implement in different ways the benefits which the treaties purported to give to them.
I think this bill, as the Minister said, has its origin in the requests made over the years by various Indian bands and others who are equally concerned about the welfare and advancement of our Indian people. In particular it was the subject of discussion in the joint committee. At page 13 of the report of the Committee, the very last recommendation, the following appears:
An Indian Claims Commission should be established to hear the British Columbia and Oka Indian land questions and other matters, and that the cost of counsel to Indians for the two land questions specified above be borne by the federal treasury.
I emphasize the use of the words "and other matters", because in the course of delibera-
June 21, 1965

Indian Claims Commission tions and during several days in July 1961, when the steering committee wrestled with the question of what should be included in the report for presentation to the main Committee, there had been suggestions by the officials of the Department that the Claims Commission should be limited to the two issues Of British Columbia and Oka Indian land questions. However, Members of the Committee, including hon. Members of the other place felt that this was insufficient; that there were other issues that remained to be settled and until these claims were resolved we could not be said to have done justice to the obligations, both legal and moral, which lay on our shoulders with respect to the Indian people of Canada. I want to make that quite plain because in concluding my remarks I want to point out the reason for the inclusion of the words "and other matters", and to emphasize and underline that certain areas of dispute should be included in this legislation or we have not lived up to our obligations.
We can consider the provisions of this bill later, but this discussion in committee gives me an opportunity to urge the inclusion of certain issues and questions which may or may not be in the bill. The Minister has not made it quite plain in this respect, and of course we will not know until we see the bill.
During the course of the last year or so there have been a number of court decisions which have brought up and emphasized the problems which still exist, particularly with regard to the rights of Indian people under the treaties which were entered into between the Federal Government and various Indian peoples. I am not going to go into all of them because this is not the time or the forum, but I should like to refer briefly to three. I will not infringe the rules, Mr. Chairman, and discuss the merits of these issues; I simply refer to them because some of them are still sub judice.
There is the recent decision of the magistrate's court in Saskatchewan declaring that what is known as the medicine chest clause in the treaties was sufficient on which to found a claim by the Indian people to receive certain medical and hospitalization privileges without having to pay for them. This in turn could cast a responsibility upon the Federal Government. Then there was a case in British Columbia involving traditional hunting and trapping rights which I think is still in the process of appeal. There may have been an abandonment of the appeal, but as far as I

know it is still being considered. Third, there was the George case in Ontario where an appeal court decided, at least by inference, that the Migratory Birds Convention Act did not apply to Indians, a decision which has subsequently, in effect, been cancelled by a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in the "lame duck" or Sikyea case.
These issues involve consideration of a number of treaties, and I am going to refer briefly to the treaties known as Nos. 1 to 11, involving all parts of western Canada save a large area of British Columbia, and parts of the northern areas in the Northwest Territories. They also involve a part of Ontario, e (4:20 p.m.)
A consideration of these treaties and the decisions of the courts, I submit, introduces a completely new element into the question of how we must fulfil our obligations to the Indian people of Canada. I precede my statement by referring to the Sikyea case, a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada which in effect has declared that the treaties in question can no longer be considered as having any validity when the Parliament of Canada acting within the course of its authority has legislated. In other words these treaties-and there are citations which bear me out in this regard-are not more than promises made from time to time by Government officials, from the year 1870 up to I believe 1922 or 1923, purporting to act on behalf of the Government of Canada, when actually they have no solemnity or validity in view of the fact that the Government has seen fit to legislate in a way which is prejudicial and contrary to these respective agreements.
As a matter of fact I believe I am justified in making this statement. If these treaties were in fact agreements between private individuals, under the laws relating to the interpretation of contracts every one of them would be declared completely invalid in so far as the Indian people are concerned. In the first place, there have been elements of undue influence. The Government was dealing with people who were then its wards. In many cases they were illiterate and unacquainted with the legal phraseology used and completely unaware of the consequences of treaties they signed. These were agreements which were improvident and were signed in exchange for a few thousand dollars in respect of each, plus a few thousand dollars paid each year in respect of all areas except the Northwest Territories, plus
June 21, 1965	COMMONS
a suit of clothes, medals and a flag to the Indians involved, purporting to quiet the title to the Federal Government of that vast area of Canada lying west of the Great Lakes, excluding a large part of the Province of British Columbia.
To illustrate my point that this was improvident, unconscionable and against national justice, I should like to refer to the terms of a later treaty which was signed in 1922 or 1923 by which the Indians, having already transferred to the Federal Government such rights as they had in their lands, gave up their traditional fishing and hunting rights in a comparatively small part of the country, for which they received half a million dollars. Contrast that with the paltry amounts paid to the various Indian bands and the amounts paid on a yearly basis to the Indians under treaties signed during the last half of the nineteenth century.
I think that is ample proof of my proposition that these agreements were improvident, and that if they formed the basis of private agreement between two parties any court would set them aside as being completely contrary to the interests of one of the parties. The treaties were fraudulent, in that they were accompanied by promises and statements by officials made, I believe, in perfectly good faith that the promises would be kept, but made under circumstances which would indicate that there could not be that 100 per cent compliance which should be essential in treating agreements between parties such as the Federal Government on one side and Indians or small groups of Indian people on the other.
I referred for example to Treaty No. 8, which I happen to know, and which covers an area in which I live of some 100,000 square miles. That treaty was accompanied by a report of the Commissioners who were present and saw it signed. In the course of this report the Commissioners in reporting to the Superintendent General or the Minister in charge of Indian Affairs made this statement:
Our chief difficulty was the apprehension that the hunting and fishing privileges were to be curtailed. The provision in the treaty under which ammunition and twine is to be furnished went far in the direction of quieting the fears of the Indians, for they admitted that it would be unreasonable to furnish the means of hunting and fishing if laws were to be enacted which would make hunting and fishing so restrictive as to render it impossible to make a livelihood by such pursuits. But over and above the provision, we had to solemnly assure them that only such laws as to hunting and fishing as were in the interest of the Indians and were found necessary in order to protect the fish and fur bearing animals would be made, and that
DEBATES	2689
Indian Claims Commission they would be as free to hunt and fish after the treaty as they would be if they never entered into it.
Mr. Chairman, statements of that kind, in the light of what has happened since and in the light of the decision in the Sikyea case, by which the highest court of this country has confirmed that the Migratory Birds Convention Act, passed as a matter of fact some years before the last treaties were signed, are as fraudulent as it is possible to be in the case of an agreement of this kind. It is quite obvious that the rights to hunt and fish and trap have been curtailed not only as a result of increased settlement and the coming of civilization to many parts of Canada-this is something with which we cannot quarrel- but actually by Federal legislation, and that these are rights that have been substantially diminished or lost.
I maintain that if these had been agreements between two private parties any court would set them aside as being invalid and improvident, having in mind the relationship of the parties and what actually passed between them.
I have referred to the Sikyea case as a firm illustration of the decision of the Appellate Court of the Northwest Territories, and this has relation to Treaties Nos. 8 and 11, which is in effect a declaration that these treaties cannot be regarded as anything more than undertakings and promises, and not binding legally on the government; and that as such, according to the convention and constitution of practice which prevails, any Parliament is free to alter and change them. It is all very well for various courts to state, as has been stated from time to time, that the Federal Government would not change them; the fact remains that there have been changes and that Indian people have no reason to accept the statements and promises made at this time unless the legislation contains within its four corners stringent and adequate safeguards for these people is respect of those treaties. We must allay their alarm, wipe out their fears and make sure that they approach further negotiations in a far better spirit than has been the case in the past.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
1 do not wish to take up too much more time, as I know other Members want to participate in this debate, but I want to make this point quite clear. I suggest to the Minister and the committee that this legislation will be inadequate; it will be defective and insufficient unless it contains a provision that will permit the Indian people, either in-
June 21, 1965

Indian Claims Commission dividually or in groups, to use this particular means of seeking recourse and remedy for breaches of treaties, even though these treaties can be legally broken by the Federal Government. The solemn responsibility resting upon the Government under these conditions cannot be discharged unless at this time legislation of this kind contains a provision that Indian people who have suffered in any way through failure to comply with these treaties will have an opportunity to seek recourse.
I understand, of course, that an interdepartmental committee has been established which is considering the effect of one of the decisions. I am not going to anticipate what the final decision may be in connection with the so-called medicine chest case, but there is no doubt that the Sikyea case is going to weigh very heavily upon those who carry the onus of trying to establish the rights of Indian people in that litigation. But when all these things have been decided I should like to see this legislation in such a state- it can only be done by enacting proper provisions now-that Indian people who have suffered injustices will be able to seek recourse through this means and not have to wait for this legislation to be amended later, for the Indian Act to be amended or for other provisions to be introduced.
I recognize that the facts of life are such that it may be difficult and may take a long time to bring this legislation back and secure amendments, and I suggest to the Minister that this should be an open-ended type of act. If the bill does not include such a clause I submit there should be a provision-I am not going to suggest at this time how it should read because we will have to wait until we see the bill-to the effect that people who have suffered prejudice in any way through failure to comply with the treaties will be free to apply, through an interlocutory application to a single member of the commission, for the right to have their case ventilated, considered and a decision made. I also suggest that any such provision should not be construed in a strictly legal sense.
The Minister is a lawyer, and I know he will recognize the difficulties facing the Indian people when they have to undergo the expense involved in the gathering of evidence to prepare a case for trial in the first instance for a subsequent appeal and for the final appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. The length of time that has to be taken in considering a matter of this kind is also something which must be taken into account.

I suggest this is an admirable vehicle by which with the proper type of wording it will be possible, after final decisions have been reached in the existing cases involving treaty rights and the obligations of the government, either in honour or in law, for the Indian people to have their grievances remedied without the necessity of having to go through the courts. I suggest this is the right vehicle for it, and I hope if such a provision is not now in the bill something will be done to meet my request before the bill is presented to us.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT. DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have no hesitation whatever in expressing my own view that the question placed before the House in the resolution now under consideration is the most important matter which this Parliament will consider during its entire period of life. I listened attentively to the remarks just made by the hon. Member for Peace River, and it is evident that he shares my concern that when we see the legislation it will be adequate to do the kind of job that needs to be done. He dwelt at some length on the situation in the part of the country with which he is most familiar, and later in my own remarks I may try to illustrate the need for adequate legislation by some reference to the situation in the part of the country with which I am more familiar.
First of all, however, I should like to mention something on which the hon. Member for Peace River only touched in passing. It is because of my concern about this aspect of the legislation that I make the statement that in my view this legislation is the most significant of any we are likely to have presented to us in this Parliament. I feel that what comes out of the legislation being introduced by this resolution will have an impact upon Canada's stature as a nation in the family of nations for generations to come. In my opinion its effect for good or ill will last long after the current dialogue between the two so-called founding races of this country will have been fogotten; and the effect of the studies and findings of such bodies as the B and B commission will be dwarfed when contrasted with the significance of the bodies that will be established under this legislation. I am referring to the proposal set out in the resolution for an Indian Claims Commission and an Indian Claims Appeal Court.
If the two bodies proposed in the resolution do not do the job that it is quite obvious the hon. Member for Peace River hopes they
June 21, 1965

will do, and that I and I think most other Members of the House hope they will do, then Canada will no longer have any right or justification to hold its head high in the modern world in which we live. I think we have to view this proposal in the light of the realities of the world in which we now live; a world in which the peoples of European stock, who for so long were dominant, are now on the defensive; a world in which we are seeing the emergence of races and peoples so long subservient into a position where their right to freedom and self determination is being achieved and respected.
We have only to think of the discussions that have been going on in London between the Prime Ministers of the various Commonwealth nations to understand how significant it is that if we in Canada are to be a self respecting member of the Commonwealth we have got to take action within our own borders paralleling in statesmanship the action taken in recent years by the United Kingdom in permitting formerly subservient peoples of Asia and Africa to emerge as fully independent and equal partners in the Commonwealth of Nations. For as long as I can remember there has been a great deal of sentiment in Canada in favour of the people of such countries as India obtaining their freedom. This arises in part, of course, out of our own experience in emerging from colonial status. But it does seem to me that over the years we have taken a free and easy attitude of support for the freedom of the people of India and of other countries in Africa which have now become members of the Commonwealth, while at the same time we have been completely blind with regard to what we have been doing in respect of the freedom we won and which gives us our national stature. It seems now that for far too long we Canadians have been more concerned with the removal of the mote from the eye of Britain than we have with the removal of the beam in our own eye.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that our days are numbered; that the world is not much longer going to remain unaware of the situation that exists in this country in respect of the original inhabitants, whom we have so largely replaced. They are no longer going to hold us in the kind of esteem in which we are held in many quarters of the world, and which in reality we do not deserve.
I think we have to consider what this legislation is going to mean in the context of the North American situation, which is not
Indian Claims Commission exactly parallel to that which has prevailed in Africa or in Asia. I believe it is probably fair to say that even the Indian people themselves do not expect those of us of European descent to withdraw from this continent in the way Europeans have agreed to withdraw from many of the areas in Africa and Asia. It seems to me that the job that has to be done by this legislation, in effect, is parallel to the job which has been done by Britain in granting India her freedom and independence, and in following through by granting various other one-time colonial groups their freedom and independence.
It should be the function of the body set up by this legislation to do that job in the context of the realities of the situation, and with the objective of achieving for the Canadian people the same restoration of their basic freedoms that is being achieved by some of the other peoples in the world today. I think it is true, Mr. Chairman, to say that in the part of Canada from which I come what has happened is perhaps of more recent memory than it is in some of the eastern parts of this continent. It is possible for those of us who live in British Columbia today to talk to people who at least can tell us the stories they have heard first hand from their grandfathers as to how the European infiltration and occupation took place. For that reason perhaps we may be able to see more vividly the results of this than may be the case in the Atlantic half of the continent, where the process took place a greater number of years ago.
Perhaps I can best put before the Members of the Committee my own feeling and understanding by making some refences to a book written by one Gilbert Malcolm Sproat, whose name has now become associated with a very beautiful lake close to where I live. This book was published in London in 1868 and is entitled "Scenes and Studies of Savage Life". If the Committee will permit me I should like to quote somewhat liberally from this book, because I have not come across anything else in my own reading on the questions that are involved that sets out quite so vividly just how the Europeans went about their business, at least in the coastal areas of British Columbia. In the preface to this book Mr. Sproat says:
I did not intend, originally, to publish these observations and have made no attempt, now, at literary ornament in producing them. Any value found in these pages will consist, I think, in their freshness and minuteness of detail, as well as in the more special consideration of social feelings, moral and intellectual characteristics and religious
June 21, 1965

Indian Claims Commission notions-matters which travellers among savages, ordinarily, have not full opportunity to do justice to.
This book, which was produced about 100 years ago, indicates to me at least the state of mind of the Europeans of that time, when Britain was at the height of her colonial empire, and perhaps some of the contrasts in the terms we might be prepared to use today in discussing some of these questions. Mr. Sproat indicates, and I am quoting again:
I did not merely pass through the country. The information which I give concerning their language, manners, customs, and ways of life, is not from memory, but from memoranda, written with a pencil on the spot-in the hut, in the canoe, or in the deep forest; and afterwards verified or amended by my own further researches-
Then in the first chapter, Mr. Chairman, he describes his entry into that part of Vancouver Island where I now make my home. He sets out his experiences which led to the establishment of the first export saw mill in British Columbia, in these terms:
In August, I860, I entered Nitinaht, or Barclay Sound, on the outside, or western, coast of Vancouver Island, with two armed vessels, Woodpecker and Meg M-errilies, manned by about fifty men, who accompanied me for the purpose of taking possession of the district now called Albemi, a name taken from the Spanish navigator who first discovered the inlet at the head of the Sound. Reaching the entrance to this inlet, we sailed for twenty miles up to the end of it-as up a natural canal-three-quarters of a mile wide and very deep, bordered by rocky mountains, which rose high on both sides almost perpendicularly from the water. The view, as we advanced up this inlet from the sea, was shut in behind and before us, making the prospect like that from a mountain lake. At the end of this singular canal, the rocky sides of which appear to have been smoothed by a continued action of moving ice upon their surface, and which itself gives an idea of having been the furrow of a mighty glacier moving downwards toward the sea, tne high land on the right receded from the shore, and a large bay or basin, with a river flowing into it through level wooded land, met our view. The range of hills which opened on one side formed an elbow about ten miles distant from the canal, and crossing in a direction almost at right angles to the course of the inlet, met a continuation of the other range, and thus shut in the district known to all the Indians as the famous berry-land of Somass.
Near a pretty point at one side of the bay, where there was a beach shaded by young trees, the summer encampment of a tribe of natives was to be seen. Our arrival caused a stir, and we saw their flambeaux of gumsticks flickering among the trees during the night.
In the morning I sent a boat for the chief, and explained to him that his tribe must move their encampment, as we had bought all the surrounding land from the Queen of England, and wished to occupy the site of the village for a particular purpose. He replied that the land belonged to themselves, but that they were willing to sell it. The price not being excessive, I paid him what was

asked-about twenty pounds worth of goods- for the sake of peace, on condition that the whole people and buildings should be removed next day. But no movement was then made, and as an excuse it was stated that the children were sick. On the following day the encampment was in commotion; speeches were made, faces blackened, guns and pikes got out, and barricades formed. Outnumbered as we were, ten to one, by men armed with muskets and our communication with the sea cut off by the impossibility of sailing steadily down the Albemi Canal (the prevalent breeze blowing up it), there was some cause for alarm had the natives been resolute. But being provided, fortunately, in both vessels with cannon-of which the natives at that time were much afraid-they, after a little show of force on our side, saw that resistance would be inexpedient, and began to move from the spot.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Then he goes on:
Two or three days afterwards, when the village had been moved to another place, not far distant, I visited the principal house at the new encampment, with a native interpreter.
"Chiefs of the Seshahts," said I on entering, "are you well; are your women in health; are your children hearty; do your people get plenty of fish and fruits?"
"Yes," answered an old man, "our families are well, our people have plenty of food; but how long this will last we know not. We see your ships, and hear things that make our hearts grow faint. They say that more King-George-men will soon be here, and will take our land, our firewood, our fishing grounds; that we shall be placed on a little spot, and shall have to do everything according to the fancies of the King-George-men."
"Do you believe all this?" I asked.
"We want your information," said the speaker.
"Then," answered I, "it is true that more King-George-men (as they call the English) are coming: they will soon be here; but your land will be bought at a fair price."
"We do not wish to sell our land nor our water; let your friends stay in their own country."
To which I rejoined: "My great chief, the high chief of the King-George-men, seeing that you do not work your land, orders that you shall sell it. It is of no use to you. The trees you do not need; you will fish and hunt as you do now, and collect firewood, planks for your houses, and cedar for your canoes. The white man will give you work, and buy your fish and oil."
"Ah, but we don't care to do as the white men wish."
"Whether or not," said I, "the white men will come. All your people know that they are your superiors; they make the things which you value. You cannot make muskets, blankets, or bread. The white men will teach your children to read printing, and to be like themselves."
"We do not want the white man. He steals what we have. We wish to live as we are."
These words I have quoted, and many others in this book, have brought home to me more forcefully than anything else the real situation, and what is really behind the so-called land question in B.C.; and though I would like to say a good deal more on the
June 21, 1965
subject, I hope they have indicated to the committee in some small way why I feel this is the most significant piece of legislation that we will be asked to discuss in this Parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be very brief, but I do want to commend the Government for bringing this legislation before us. I hope it will be passed as quickly as possible and that the joint committee it proposes will deal with its work expeditiously.
Now that we have reached this stage I hope we shall soon correct some of the errors of the past and enable the Indians to benefit from claims which have been held up for many years.
So far as compensation is concerned I hope it will be generous, because many acts committed in the past need review and correction. I am constrained to ask that the benefit of the doubt be placed on the side of the Indian, because so often we are not too relative in our thinking concerning the spending of money. A few years ago we did not hesitate for one minute to give the Canada Council $100 million, and since that time we have given it many more millions of dollars.
Based on this and other expenditures by the Federal Government, I hope the recommendations made in connection with compensation will be made from the point of view of dollars and cents, and that we will not be niggardly. I hope the main task of the commission will be quickly and effectively undertaken, and that the life of the commission will be short so the Indians can soon have the redress which has been long owed them.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the
next few minutes I should like to express our satisfaction with this resolution providing for the setting up of an Indian Claims Commission.
I think that this bill, which we will have the opportunity of considering in detail, comes at an opportune time and especially that it will meet the wishes of the Indian bands which have requested for a long time, every time we have met with the chiefs or Indian band authorities, such an agency through which they could plead their case before the federal government.
I think a grave injustice was done to the Indian people when they were confined within a reserve under the supervision of a manager called a reserve administrator.
As far as I know from my own constituency-I am not speaking about Indians in
Indian Claims Commission other provinces-Indians are often the victims of dealings which could hardly be called fair on the part of this reserve manager who, of course, is always a white man.
I myself found that Indians had complained in vain on many occasions and they certainly had legitimate grievances against the present administration of Indian reserves.
The worse part of it was that those Indians had no way of making themselves heard by the federal authorities, except through a branch that has so much to look after throughout Canada that it does not matter much when 10 or 15 small Indian families raise their voices in the Roberval area. I myself asked the minister to conduct inquiries. And what happened? The present chief of the Indian reserve himself was asked to do it. Can you imagine? When 10 or 15 families have a legitimate complaint against the chief and finally succeed in having an inquiry set up by the federal Indian Affairs branch, we are told that the chief is conducting the inquiry. Imagine the results.
I am very happy for the people of the Indian reserve of the riding of Roberval that this commission will be established. I hope it will be independent and that a great many of its members will be Indians so that it can provide benefits to the Indian people and that it will not again be influenced somehow by politics. When the survival of a people is at stake, it is not time to play party politics. The Indian people deserve consideration because they have been very patient up to now.
Since I have been sitting here, I have made three or four interventions myself to suggest to the government means of interesting Indians or of giving a little more meaning to their lives, because if you spoke with chiefs, you would find family heads telling you that the worst thing for them is to feel that they are useless.
Some people complain that those Indians are government pensioners. They do not want to be government pensioners, they do not want to be useless in a country like Canada. The government should assist them as it assists any other association, it should help them in matters of tourism. As I said a moment ago, I am only speaking for the Indians in my riding because the only way to help the Indians of Pointe-Bleue is by promoting the tourist industry. You have there the most beautiful tourist attraction in the area but nothing has been done about

June 21, 1965

Indian Claims Commission it, even though fully qualified personnel could be found within the reserve itself. If only the federal government agreed to spend a few thousand dollars to develop the tourist industry in the area. But, unfortunately, nothing is being done.
I have made three or four requests in that respect, but still nothing is being done, except forwarding the meagre pay cheques to the Indians, every month, but that does not help the economy of the area and yet, the Indians themselves would be so proud to participate in the development of Canada.
I have gone to the reserve and all those I have met said they had no way of expressing their views. I think that, through this commission, the Indian reserve will be able to submit its requests and express its views directly to the government agencies; the Indians have marvelous suggestions to make, but nothing can be done about them unless the government is aware of them.
I will no doubt have the opportunity of dealing with this again when this bill is before the house, but I wish to commend the government for introducing this resolution and I hope that the proposed legislation will be wide enough in scope to include any question which is important to the future of the Indian people in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have
listened with keen interest to the previous speakers and I think we can see that we are all thinking along similar lines and are, at the present at least, in full agreement, which is something new in the House of Commons. I would just like to say, as one who hunted, fished and trapped with the Indians in my younger days, that I am certainly very interested in and extremely pleased to see this resolution being brought in providing for the establishment of an Indian Claims Commission. Such a Claims Commission is very important to Indians in the various parts of Canada, and I believe it will be of significant importance to the Indians of the Six Nations Reserve, who over the years have advanced their claims against the Crown.
The Six Nations Indian Reserve, one of the best known bands of Indians in Canada, is only a short distance from my own home and I have many personal friends there. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I would like to bring to your attention a few historical facts about the Six Nations Indians and something about their claims. The Six Nations Indians have had a

long and historic association with the Crown. In fact, they fought on the side of the Crown in the War of Independence and as a result were invited to come to Canada after the close of the war. The reserve was purchased from the Mississauga Indians. It ran along the banks of the Grand River and extended some six miles on either side. It took in a large area of ground, something like 700,000 acres. The grant of land was made by Sir Frederick Haldimand in 1784 and the reserve was confirmed to the Indians by Governor Simcoe in 1793. It consisted of Haldimand, Brant, Waterloo and Wellington Counties. However, that huge territory has slowly been disposed of and today they have a reservation of some
40,000	acres in the Townships of Tuscarora and Oneida.
I would also like to point out that we have some very outstanding persons from the Six Nations Reserve. As I am a person who has been interested in athletics over the years, as many hon. Members know, the first name that comes to my mind is Tom Longboat, the great long distance runner whose achievements brought not only fame to himself but to his country, his people and the Six Nations Indians in particular. Then, of course, there is that one and only poetess, Pauline Johnson, the poetess whose beautiful and stirring ballads have been learned by generations of Canadian school children, and I sincerely hope always will be learned by Canadian school children. In the field of science there is Dr. G. C. Monture, noted Canadian mineralogist, who is another outstanding Six Nations Indian. Then there is the late Magistrate Martin who dispensed justice for both Indian and non-Indian; he was also from the Six Nations near Brantford. There are others, Mr. Chairman, but I will not enumerate them all. I am certain, from the few examples I have given of outstanding people who have come from this one reserve, that there are many Indians who will be able to contribute to the work of this Commission if given the opportunity. While the appointment of an Indian would have been possible under the previous bill, I am sure hon. Members will agree that requiring the appointment of at least one Indian will meet with the favour of Indians across Canada. I cannot stress this too much. Indeed, there were many briefs from Indians and others which suggested that this be done, and I sincerely hope the Minister will see that it is done.
June 21, 1965

[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I also hope that the bill will make provision for the hearing of various kinds of claims. The Six Nations have advanced claims in the past, and I have in front of me an article from the Ottawa Journal for December 6, 1949, describing how members of the reserve were claiming compensation for part of the reserve which, they alleged, had been disposed of by the Governor to the old Grand River Navigation Company in the 1830's. These were just clear grants, by the way, without compensation. Without doubt this bill should provide, and I sincerely hope it will, that the claims may be brought where lands were disposed of by the Crown without payment of compensation, or where the compensation was not just and reasonable. There must be some consideration along these lines of thought; you cannot go exactly to the rule of the law itself.
If such provision were made it would meet the kind of claim that the Six Nations have put forward in the past.
In addition the Six Nations have alleged that about $160,000 of their trust funds were invested in worthless Grand River Navigation Company shares by the Province of Canada, and lost to them. I sincerely hope that this bill will make it possible to bring a claim which alleges that band funds have been improperly used.
It appears to me, Mr. Chairman, that a means is being found by this legislation to deal with the old claims which have been of concern to Indians of the Six Nations reserve, and of course right across Canada, which for one reason or another they were unable to get settled in the ordinary courts. Indians in Canada, and the Six Nations Indians in particular, place great weight upon their treaties and agreements made with the Crown. They regard these agreements as solemn contracts to be honoured by both Indians and Crown, and I should add justly so. It certainly makes one feel good that at this time we have a Minister, the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, who truly and sincerely, as I know all hon. Members feel, has the problems of the Indians at heart. With a Minister like this and with this Commission being set up I am sure something is going to be done at least.
As far as the Indians of the Six Nations reserve are concerned, it is interesting to note that the Haldimand grant by which the reserve was granted contained the following phrase:
-which them and their prosperity are to enjoy forever.

Indian Claims Commission
The Simcoe deed which confirmed the land grant contained the following expression:
-giving and granting, and by these presents confirming to the said Chiefs, warriors, women and people of the Six Nations and their heirs, the full and entire possession, use, benefit and advantage of the said district or territory, to be held and enjoyed by them in the most free and ample manner, and according to the several customs and usages of them the said Chiefs, warriors, women and people of the said Six Nations.
That is pretty plain, is it not? We cannot get around that, and I am sure we are not going to try to. I have quoted this extract to show the nature of some of the undertakings into which the Crown entered.
Some Indians have claimed that their treaties or agreements have been broken, as was stated by some of the previous speakers. Where there are cases of this I sincerely hope that the bill will allow the Indians to bring such matters before the Commission to seek redress. I feel very sure, the way things are going, that this will be done.
There is no doubt in our minds, and we have to face this, that the Commission will have a very complex job to do, as so much of its work will be to try and determine what happened years ago, yes even before Confederation. It will need to become familiar with many of the old documents such as the ones from which I have just quoted. It will need to do research into the history of Indian tribes and their relations with government over the years. Many investigations will be required. I certainly believe the Commission should have some researchers on its staff who will be able to do this and gather information and documents for the use of the Commission. I hope that under the bill the Commission will be able to conduct investigations, and perhaps others will be designated to do this. The Members of the Commission should also visit various places across the country to hear the complaints of Indians and to collect evidence from them, thus saving the Indians travelling long distances.
It is all very fine, of course, for the Commission to do this, and we want them to do it, but what about the Indian himself? Is he in the same position to acquire all this information? Therefore I should like to suggest that the Indians may need help to get necessary documents some of which may be in the Public Archives of Canada, others in the provincial archives, and still others in various departments of Government. Some of the reserves were established long before Confederation, as I have previously stated, and
June 21. 1965

Indian Claims Commission I hope that the Commission will make some arrangement whereby all these old documents are made available to the Indians. If the Commission is as sincere as we feel it is going to be, then they should make a special effort to see that the Indians have every bit of information possible so that these claims may be judged and dealt with properly.
I feel very sure that this legislation now being brought in will be a sincere attempt by the Parliament of today to make good some of the losses suffered by the Indians in the past. A great many of these losses were mentioned just a few moments ago. Therefore I believe this legislation should be supported and I hope that the Commission will be appointed as soon as possible, so it can get started on its important work. I believe we all recognize that mistakes have been made, but given a Commission which will be guided by the principles of equity and justice some of these old claims, such as those of the Six Nations Indians, can be finally settled.
I would hope that where compensation is received as a result of a claim it will be used to develop the reserves and to build them up to where the people can be fully selfsupporting, a state of affairs greatly lacking today. There is some excellent farming land on the Six Nations Indian reserve, and if they put forward a claim which is successful I would hope to see more put into agricultural development, as well as industrial and other development on the reserve, employing local residents, the Indians themselves generally raising the economic well being of people on the reserve, and on reserves right across Canada.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I would hope that as a result of this legislation the Indians will feel at last that they have been justly treated and that the mistakes that may have been made in the past have been rectified in a manner which honour and good conscience dictate.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT. DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to take only a few minutes to comment on the opening statement of the Minister, and to express some of the worries I have outside the provisions which the Minister said would be in the bill.
[DOT] (5 :20 p.m.)
It seems to me that the provisions as outlined in the resolution and as briefly elaborated on by the Minister are fine, but perhaps I can be forgiven if I say that what we in the Opposition want are assurances. We have not seen the legislation yet and while I espouse 
the glowing remarks which the previous speaker has made in reference to the Minister, and while from my experience I am reasonably confident in his attitude toward the problems of Indian people in general, I should like this overlaid with some kind of assurance given by the Minister in this House, when he speaks in closing the debate on this resolution, that the outstanding claims of the Indian people are going to be settled in a fair and equitable manner.
The Minister said that the Indian Claims Commission legislation will go a long way toward renewing or re-establishing the trust of the Indian people. This is not going to be an easy task or something that is going to be done by any single piece of legislation. In view of the Indian's experience with the white man in the past, he would be foolish to trust the white man, and I believe it is going to take many years and depend on the first few steps taken by this Commission before the Indian people will trust the white man.
I can think of no better illustration of the situation than by quoting the remarks of Lieutenant Governor Morris in speaking to the Indian people of Qu'Appelle when Treaty No. 4 was signed. He was then the Lieutenant Governor of the Northwest Territories. This is what he told the Indian people, and I hope Members of this House will listen and relate these remarks to what has happened since. He said:
Therefore, the promises we have to make to you are not for today only but for tomorrow,-not only for you but for your children born and unborn, and the promises we make will be carried out as long as the sun shines above and water flows in the ocean.
If the Minister thinks that one piece of legislation will undo the wrong, keeping that quotation in mind, and I am being slightly facetious, he is entirely wrong. Surely none of us would think that the legislation now before us is going to undo the damage which has been done by statements of that kind made at the time of the signing of these treaties. Those treaties were signed, and the promises were made, only to get the Indians to stop shooting and scalping. In nearly every part of the country the treaties were broken before the ink was dry. The words used by the negotiators were nothing but lies. I suppose the attitude adopted by many in these days, and we have come a long way since then is much the same, that it is quite a thing to put something over on the redskins. Moreover, when Lieutenant Governors made statements of that kind, following which the treaties and promises were broken, then
June 21, 1965	COMMONS
indeed as the hon. Member for Peace River has said, these are fraudulent documents, and at no time did the negotiators in my opinion ever intend to live up to them. The Indian people are conscious of that fact.
A few years ago a Royal Commission was set up to investigate the treaties in respect of the Northwest Territories, which were never fulfilled. I should like to read a few sentences from a report in respect of what some Indian people said:
At a number of meetings Indians who claimed to have been present at the time when the Treaties were signed stated that they definitely did not recall hearing about the land entitlement in the Treaties. They explained that poor interpreters were used and these interpreters urged the Indians to sign, saying "It will be good for you." It was emphasized that their chiefs and head men signed even though they did not know what the Treaties contained because the Treaty parties included high government and religious officials whom the Indians trusted to look after their interests. When the Chairman pointed out that the chiefs of each band, among others, had received copies of the treaties the Indians replied that they were published in complicated English and they could not understand them.
We now have a basis for suspicion, rather than trust, which goes back many years. I say these things not to deprecate the legislation in any way-quite the contrary-but merely to point out that there is a danger in suggesting that any piece of legislation is a final solution to the Indian problem, because this problem goes back hundreds of years and is rooted in mistrust.
I hope the vehicle provided by this legislation will obviate the necessity of marches such as that which took place on the Alberta Legislature a few months ago. At that time as a result of prompting by several individuals who had a beautiful sense of political timing the Indian people of the Hay Lakes area of Northern Alberta marched on the Provincial Legislature. It is significant that this march took place on a day when a bill to grant the Indian franchise was before the Provincial Legislature. The timing was no accident, and the hurried meetings and the subsequent dispatch of senior officials to the Hay Lakes area generally has resulted, it seems to me, in there being more Government officials in that area than Indian people, with a desire to redress their grievances. As a friend of mine remarked, all this proves is that the price of baubles has gone up. In the old days trinkets were used by the white man to placate the Indians. The price has now gone up, and the articles include saw mills, D-6 caterpillars and so on.
DEBATES	2697
Indian Claims Commission
It is to be hoped that such a vehicle as a Claims Commission will provide an opportunity for the redress of grievances, real or imagined, on the part of the Indian people. This legislation may well have another advantage which I think should not be overlooked. In the minds of many non-Indians the Government is pampering the Indian people by giving them more than they are entitled to. I am sure the Minister has been faced with the suggestion that the Indian people are being pampered and that in some way they are getting all sorts of things they should not get. Such a suspicion is detrimental to the Indian people themselves, and interferes with their being able to fill a proper role in the field of employment. There may be a side advantage to the establishment of an Indian Claims Commission in this regard. If that Commission can listen to the evidence and adjudicate in fairness it will do a great service for the cause of Indian welfare, social and economic.
I was pleased to hear the Minister state that a joint committee of the House and Senate is to be set up. Like other speakers,
I have a great deal of respect for the work that has been done by Members of the other place in respect of Indian affairs. I have too, a great deal of respect for the kind of knowledge that certain Members of the other place can bring to this kind of work. I was delighted when the Minister hinted during an interjection that the Committee would be faced with a deadline of three months within which it must report. That hint makes the Minister's announcement that there will be a committee established even more interesting and exciting.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
It was unfortunate that the Minister could not be more elaborate in his statement regarding the resolution on the order paper. The resolution indicates that the legislation will provide assistance to Indian bands in preparing and pursuing claims. When the Minister closes the debate on the resolution I hope he will be able to answer some of these questions. I hope that the provision of assistance in preparing and pursuing claims will include the hiring of independent legal counsel for the Indian people where necessary, and that departmental officers, even departmental legal officers, will not be advising the Indian people on the forms that are to be filled out or the legal ritual they are to follow. I cannot urge this too strongly on the Minister. In doing so I am in no way deprecating or holding suspect the approach
June 21. 1965

Indian Claims Commission of the officials of the branch; on the contrary, I am quite happy with them and trust them implicitly. But 1 do feel it is important to make it clear to the Indian people that they may engage legal counsel and that if financial problems arise in the payment of counsel the Government will be prepared to assist them in some way.
I endorse the suggestion of the previous speaker, which is one I intended to make, that the terms of reference of the Commission include the ability to travel and take the Commission to the people. This is particularly important in the more remote areas of Canada because otherwise there will be no real satisfaction of the grievances of the Indian people.
I want to come to my main point now. I am concerned lest the proposed legislation will not include any redress of the basic grievance of the Indian people of the Yukon and Northwest Territories. The hon. Member for Peace River referred to this matter in passing and I want to mention it again. Hon. Members may know that there are two areas of Canada where there are no Indian reserves, the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories. There is a good reason why there are no reserves there. The treaties signed with the northern Indian people were never lived up to, even the basic requirement of giving the Indian people certain parcels of land which they could hold.
I am not urging for one second the setting up of Indian reserves in those areas. On the basis of our experience in the south I do not think this would be a wise move, nor do I believe the Indian people in the north want it. But the fact that there are no reservations there, which in my opinion is a good thing in itself, results from the complete failure of the Crown and succeeding Governments to live up to the provisions of Treaty No. 8 signed on June 21, 1899. That treaty covered parts of northern Alberta and parts of the Northwest Territories immediately south of Great Slave Lake. It involved a total area of some 480,000 square miles. The actual cash payment made to the Indian people was $26,974 or roughly $27,000.
Just in passing may I say it would probably be well for Canadians not to make joking remarks about the Dutch buying Manhattan island for $42, in view of the fact that we purchased almost half a million square miles from the Indians for less than $27,000. The treaty provided that for every five Indian families one square mile of land would be

set aside. This was done for those Indian people living in the northern parts of Alberta, but for some strange reason the Indian people living just north of the 60th parallel in the Northwest Territories were never given the land to which they were entitled under the treaty. It may have been an oversight, but I rather suspect they were overlooked because of the move toward selfgovernment from 1903 to 1905 that resulted in Saskatchewan and Alberta being carved out of the Northwest Territories.
Treaty No. 11, the second treaty, was signed on July 17, 1922. In effect it involved the purchase of 600,000 square miles of land in what is now the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories for just over $23,000. It too provided that the Indian people there would be given one square mile of land for every five families. This was never done. So the basic reason there are no Indian reservations in the Northwest Territories is not that it was planned that way, but results from the fact that we did not give the Indian people those things we promised them.
There are many Indian people in the north who were present when these treaties were signed. To this day they carry with them a vaguely defined but burning distrust of white officials. This has rendered the job of the Indian Affairs Branch in these parts of the north that much more difficult because the Indian people know they cannot trust the white man. They have not been able to do so since 1922, when the second treaty was signed, and they have no reason to believe they are going to be able to do so in the future. In addition, the Indians were promised that they would be able to hunt, trap and fish on unoccupied Crown land. Those were the two major provisions of the treaties affecting the northern Indians.
I want to quote a pertinent sentence from the report of Commissioner Conroy which is attached to the treaty he signed with the Indians of the Northwest Territories. He said:
The Indians seemed afraid for one thing that their liberty to hunt, trap and fish would be taken away or curtailed but were assured by me that this would not be the case.
The two main things promised the Indians of the north were the right to hunt, trap and fish at will on unoccupied Crown lands and the setting aside of land for them. Some other things were promised such as 10 axes, five handsaws, a grindstone, the necessary files and whetstones and so on but they are not
June 21, 1965

important. One of the most important provisions was that they would be given land. Today in the Northwest Territories it is practically impossible for an Indian person even to purchase the land on which his house stands. At no time were they given land. They know they were entitled to thousands and thousands of acres of land as a reserve. They know they did not get it. They also know that when they apply for title in fee simple to the land they occupy they have tremendous difficulty getting it. Not only do the Indians have trouble in this regard but everyone else in the Northwest Territories has trouble in getting title to land. However, the injustice is particularly sharp in their case because they know they have thousands of acres coming to them.
The reason I am worried that this legislation will not be a vehicle for the Indians to get redress of this grievance is that this is not the first time the unfulfilled provisions of Treaties Nos. 8 and 11 have been looked into by governments. Indeed in 1959 the former Government set up a Royal Commission to investigate the unfulfilled provisions of Treaties 8 and 11 as they apply to the Indians of the Mackenzie district. This Commission travelled about the Territory, interviewed the Indians and made some recommendations. The difficulty was that the Government did not like the recommendations it received. When I say "Government" I am including all the officials of the various branches of the Government that have to do with the administration of the Northwest Territories.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
One can see why they might not be happy with it. The Royal Commission recommended that the Indians be granted title in fee simple to the plots of land on which they now resided and the plots on which they proposed to build their homes; that a cash settlement of $20 per acre be made for each acre to which the Indians of the Mackenzie District were entitled. This would involve a multi-million dollar cash settlement because the Indians were entitled to thousands of acres. In addition to this the Commission recommended an annual payment of one half of 1 per cent of the revenue derived by the Crown from minerals, gas and oil resources in that portion of the Northwest Territories described in treaties Nos. 8 and 11.
If you total up these recommendations in dollars and cents, the Indian people could make a good case for holding up the Federal Government to the tune of $20 million for a
Indian Claims Commission lump sum settlement. When the Minister speaks to close this debate, I hope he will indicate whether or not this legislation will provide a vehicle for satisfying these two basic claims of the Indian people of the Northwest Territories, whose treaties were never lived up to at all.
