speechtext:
I do not doubt for a moment but that every Member of the Committee has a very sincere desire to enact a law covering this general field introduced by the Minister and which will, in fact, bring justice to the native Indian people of Canada. Everyone who has spoken so far has indicated this, and from memory I do not recall anyone in the House every saying he was not favourably disposed to some mechanism whereby the native Indian people could find redress for their grievances. Perhaps we are activated by a sort of national guilt complex because of our knowledge of the unfair dealings with native Indian people in the past. It still remains a fact, however, that everyone sincerely wishes to do what is the just and correct thing.
I for one, however, am not agreeable to buying a pig in a poke, as the expression goes. I cannot bring myself to making any laudatory comments about a bill which I have not yet seen. The Minister's introductory remarks were far too brief in so far as the construction of the bill was concerned to permit the Committee to do anything else but hope that the bill does meet the sincere desires of everyone in the House for justice and consideration in this matter of dealing with the native Indian people. I know that at home some of the organizations of Indian people and some of the tribal councils were not in favour of Bill No. C-130 after it was introduced in December of 1963, I believe it was. After these people had an opportunity to examine Bill No. C-130, they were almost all of the view that if there were no changes in that bill, then they did not want to have any part of it. They did not believe it would bring favourable treatment to them or secure justice for their claims.
One of the major matters with which the native people are concerned is land. There does not seem to be any doubt but that the bill will pass speedily and that the Commission will be established speedily after the passage of the bill. One of the major things with which the Commission will be concerned, certainly with which the Indian people are concerned, will be the question of land. I believe it would be an error if the Commission were to be oriented entirely to the European
June 21, 1965

Indian Claims Commission or non-Indian concept of what is land. It would be most desirable to have, either on the Commission or attached to the Commission, someone who had an appreciation or understanding of land from the Indian point of view. The native Indian people have a concept of land, of nature and the animal world that is vastly different from that which a European has or which Canadian society in general has. I think it would be necessary to have that idea or concept reflected in the processes of the Commission in order that they could make a fair adjudication of whatever claims are presented concerning land.
Undoubtedly Bill No. C-130 is the basis of the particular bill which will be introduced following this resolution. An indication was given two years ago when the bill was introduced, and this we all desired to have, that the bill would be introduced for the purpose of evoking a response to it and suggestions for changes in it. I presume therefore that in the consideration of this resolution it would be proper for us to express ideas about Bill No. C-130, and to express the hope that many things in Bill C-130 which were objectionable to the native people will not be included in the new bill.
Then, if I could make one or two brief references to Bill No. C-130, I would say that the word "band", was somewhat objectionable. I point out that the word "band" is an English or European word which applies to a particular grouping of native Indian people, and that the word "band" was for a time alien to the Indian social structure. If the word "band", therefore, were not contained in the bill this would be helpful, and instead we might use such words as tribes or nations. I believe these words would have application to just ordinary groups of Indian people, including individual Indians. I believe these terms would be more flexible in their relation to groupings of Indian people in so far as determining the proper group to present a claim is concerned.
I believe this idea has been presented to the Minister by the Indian people, but it is felt the Commission Chairman should be someone either from the International Court of Justice or who would be qualified to sit in that court. The reason for this is that we are not dealing with ordinary matters which come before courts in the normal course of litigation, but with law which relates more to the sphere of international law. We feel, therefore, that someone from the International Court of Justice or someone qualified to sit in that court would present to the

Commission a different concept, and assure a fair and just decision of any claim. Certainly there should be Indian people represented on the Commission as well, so that someone with an intimate and inherited knowledge of Indian thinking and ideas could reflect those for the benefit of the Commission.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I also think that an anthropologist should be on the Commission, or at least employed among its staff or personnel, in order to bring that necessary profession to bear and to be able to explain, from an anthropological point of view, the historical background of Indian exploitation and ownership of land areas.
Bill No. C-130 had within it a time limit of ten years, and a time limit of two years for the presentation of claims. I am one of those who believe the Commission should expire with the last claim, or we should leave it open to a future parliament to decide when the Commission should cease to exist, because we do not have the prescience and foresight at the moment to be able to predict that ten years, or any other number of years, is sufficient to permit the hearing of all claims. In other words, there should be an open-ended tenure of office for the Commission.
When Bill No. C-130 saw the light of day a couple of years ago, the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni and I prepared a press release based upon an analysis of that bill. Perhaps with respect to what was the most important clause in that bill it might be worth while to read briefly from that press release, relating to clause 7 of Bill C-130. In that press release, which was dated December 17, 1963, the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni, who has always had an interest in Indian affairs, and I, said:
Section 7 is the worst part of the bill because it is misleading and contradictory and sets up prohibitions which, in fact, defeat the entire purpose of the bill.
It is misleading for it says that the legal rules of evidence shall not bind the Commission when it hears any claim. So far this is good because the rules of evidence demand proof or corroboration that it is not possible to provide in many of the claims which the Indian people have. But, the bill then goes on to say that there must be evidence in writing or corroborated oral evidence before the Commission can make an award.
This is a two-faced attempt to mislead the Indian people into thinking that they are going to get a fair deal from the Commission. It is double-dealing of the worst sort to say that the Commission will listen to anything presented to it but will only make an award when the evidence is in writing. It is virtually impossible to get written corroborative evidence of the wrongs which
June 21, 1965

have been thrust upon the Indian people when those wrongs took place many years ago and at a time when the Indian people could not read or write or keep written records of their dealings with non-Indians.
Section 7 further provides that the Cabinet shall have final say over the procedural rules of the Commission. This should be left to the Commission to develop without any political sanction.
Section 7 also contains the provision that the Cabinet can deny the Commission access to documents which are in the possession of the Government. This could lead to the situation where, by withholding material evidence, the Cabinet could force the Commission to decide against the Indians in any claim.
I merely quoted from that because it related to Bill C-130, and I hope the provisions of clause 7 of that bill are now sufficiently altered to remove what we had as objections at that time and which, incidentally, many Indian people at home have confirmed as being their objections also, after they had the opportunity to study the bill.
There is a long history in B.C. relating to the land question because, with one or two exceptions, there were no treaties in our province. I will not bore the Chamber with details of the attempts of the Indian people, dating back to 1913 and periodically revived since that time, except to say that it is a fact that this one question, the so-called B.C. land question, is the one with which the vast majority of native Indian people in B.C. are vitally concerned and which they want to see solved. Perhaps this Commission will be able to assist them in finding the solution.
For years our Indian people have been kept in ignorance and in isolation. As recounted by the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni in his reading of the historical accounts of missionaries and the like, in the early days they were seduced by whiskey, by land grabbers, and on occasion by missionaries, men of the cloth, who assisted the land grabbers, and in some cases assisted the rum runners and the whiskey traders to seduce the Indian people and take from them by deceit and dishonesty that which they had in their possession from time immemorial.
Now with the growing feeling in Canada about Indian affairs, with the growing feeling among Indian people that they want to participate more fully in society and that they want the solutions to their long standing grievances, I think we have a chance to balance the books somewhat, to try to undo the wrongdoing, to try to correct the errors. In fact, however, we cannot do that because we cannot turn back the clock, but under this bill I hope that at least we can get ourselves going partially in that direction.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
We can try to treat the native Indian person fairly, justly and honourably. These are terms he understands. Fairness, justice and honourable dealings have been his watchwords from time immemorial. They have not been the guide lines or the watchwords of the non-Indian in his dealings with Indians, but now we have a chance to make some alteration in that.
There is a great awakening taking place. Education, communications and increased transportation facilities are unifying the Indian people and amassing them into a single voice, whether we like it or not. We can hear this voice swell and erupt like a volcano and consume our history and background, our background of prejudice and discrimination, just the same as the voice of the coloured people in the United States is consuming prejudice and bigotry in that nation. Or we can hear the voice of the Indian people swell and become sonorous and confident, making Canada a nation of which we can be more proud than we are at the moment.
We in this Parliament have a responsibility we cannot shirk, a responsibility to be a prod either in one direction or the other. We can assist the Indian people along the lines of honourable activities, or we can by this bill turn them in the other direction so that their voice would be a volatile and disruptive voice, and I am sure none of us want that.
Under this bill we can be helpful or harmful. I, and I am sure the Minister also, hope that whatever we do it will be helpful.

I must say, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. Member will think it is later still before I am through. But as long as no one calls it ten o'clock when I am making an impressive peroration, I will not be disturbed by the faulty mechanism above. I was about to say, Mr. Speaker, that when I came here in the twenty third Parliament the President of the Privy Council had a motion on the order paper in the phraseology of mine, except that I have restricted the area geographically. It is appropriate that a Maritimer

DEBATES	June 21, 1965
should be interested in this subject because we have had close relations with the people of the West Indies for a long, long time. Perhaps it is particularly appropriate that one from an island should be discussing the economics of the people who live in other islands. But I am thinking, too, today that there is something appropriate in directing our attention to this part of our hemisphere as we follow with care and concern the deliberations in London of our own Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and his colleagues at the Commonwealth Prime Ministers Conference.
I should say that the Notice of Motion is restricted in the geographic sense. It is not that I have a lack of interest in Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and trade with those areas, but it is because the fact that the smaller islands were left out when the proposed federation collapsed, or indeed when the federation dissolved, the so-called Outer Eight, strikes me as having both a political and an economic uncertainty that should cause us, I think, as friendly neighbours, a more especial concern. The islands of Barbados, Antigua, St. Kitts, Montserrat, St. Lucia, St. Vincent and Dominica are very small. The largest of all the group, Barbados, has less than a quarter of a million people, and Montserrat has just a little over 13,000. Generally speaking they have great difficulty in maintaining an economic viability. Most of them are obtaining direct assistance in their budgetary revenues from the United Kingdom. As has been said, this is a collection of islands of 13,000 square miles, but while the area is small, the problems are large; poor soil, shortage of water, lack of proper facilities, roads and airports, shertage of skilled labour, the crying need for assistance in their effort to approach something like self-sufficiency, and a pressing problem of overpopulation. All too briefly these are some of the economic facts of life of this part of the world.
Our trade with the region has been important. Figures which I have obtained from the Department of Trade and Commerce are interesting. It is hard to sort these out, but studies have indicated that the trade of the Atlantic region with the West Indies generally, and with this area in particular, is significant. The exports to the islands I have in mind for promotion totalled $6,600,000 in 1963. In 1964 this rose to $7,986,000. This is a substantial increase. Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak in support of the motion put forward by the hon. Member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie). As a native Maritimer and a representative of the historic constituency of Westmorland, of which the City of Moncton forms a large portion, I must say that the energetic Board of Trade which we have in Moncton has visited the West Indies on various trade missions, and I am sure has been visited by West Indian delegations in Moncton. So I would wholeheartedly support this motion.
The West Indies are islands of great contrasts. Contrasts in population and language reflect their varied history, while they also differ in physical characteristics and economic development. The proposed eastern federation of the West Indies, which includes Barbados, the Leeward Islands and the Windward Islands, have a total area of 1,043 square miles and a population of 600,000, of whom
245,000	live in Barbados.
The Ministers of the islands of the proposed federation, referred to as the "Little Seven", or the "Little Eight" including Grenada, have held a number of meetings, the last in

December, 1964, to draft proposals for the formation of the federation. According to reports-and I refer to the Financial Post of December 5, 1964

there is unanimous agreement that Barbados should be the site of the capital, and that a customs union and free trade area would be established after the beginning of the federation. The economy of the islands has in the past been based on a few agricultural products, but the present aim is to diversify production.
It is very important that we should make a determined effort to help the development of the economy of these islands. We should give every assistance we can in raising the standards of living and providing more sources of employment for the people in this part of the western hemisphere. We should also take a more active part in the efforts to establish new industries in the West Indies and in the area of the proposed federation. The hon. Member for Halifax will be talking about that in a little more detail.
Canada is almost sure to receive formal requests for help in inter-island shipping, and will most probably be asked to open its doors wider to admit skilled West Indians. Free trade, of course, requires the co-operation and consent of both parties. From what I have been able to learn it would appear that some of the leaders of the West Indies have been reluctant to commit themselves to such a trading arrangement. Thisi is easily understood because tariff duties constitute a very important source of revenue for their governments, and free trade with Canada would tend to disturb their present gradual development.
It appears that most West Indians are not very enthusiastic about entering a free trade area or customs union with Canada at this time. They appear more actively engaged in promoting their economic growth and industrial expansion, and more interested in using tariffs as a means for development of new industries under their new legislation. We would have to be sure that, in proposing a free trade area with the West Indies, nonCommonwealth countries must be considered as well. Any arrangements which might be made with the proposed federation would have to take into consideration all arrangements we have at present with other parts of the West Indies. We are preparing and moving toward greater co-operation with these areas. Other speakers will elaborate on the programs of assistance and investment.
The Canada-West Indies trade is traditionally based on the exchange of food and

forestry products in exchange for sugar and its by-products. It could be suggested that possibly the entire Eastern Caribbean Federation might be brought into the area of the Canadian dollar and have them eventually leave the sterling bloc.
In all the islands there is a steady upward trend in the tourist trade which is one of the largest revenue-producing activities. This constitutes a drain on our international exchange payments, and if the West Indies were operating on the Canadian dollar this would be of great advantage to Canada. The recent announcement of a direct service by Air Canada from Halifax to Bermuda is just the first step, I would hope, in an effort to improve communications in the Maritime area and the West Indies.

The House resumed consideration in Committee of the following resolution-Mr. Nicholson-Mr. Lamoureux in the Chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the disposition of Indian claims and in relation thereto,
1.	To provide for the establishment of an Indian Claims Commission:
2.	To provide for the duties of the Commission, its decisions and awards;
3.	To provide for appeals from the decisions and awards of the Commission to an Indian Claims Appeal Court;
4.	To provide assistance to Indian bands in preparing and pursuing claims; and
5.	To enact such financial provisions as may be necessary to accomplish the purposes of the Act.
June 21, 1965

Mr. Chairman, I know all hon. Members are happy that the Government has finally taken this overdue step to create an Indian Claims Commission, which is a necessary step toward removing the distrust that remains an impediment to full participation by all Indians in Canadian life and in our present day economy.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
The resolution indicates that in providing assistance to Indian bands to prepare claims, the Government has gone far beyond what was proposed in Bill C-130, which was brought before the House last year, and we all welcome this evidence that the Government will provide this assistance. The 1961 Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons recommended that the costs of counsel in connection with these two actions before the Indian Claims Commission be borne by the Federal Treasury. The Government has now gone considerably beyond the recommendations of this joint committee by making the resolution general enough so that a wide variety of possible expenses of Indians presenting claims will be covered.
I would like to make two or three comments on the type of expenses which I feel should be covered by this proposal. Naturally legal expenses should be covered. Also, research expenses should be covered. Travelling expenses to and from Ottawa, or to wherever the Commission may be sitting, should be covered. I would go even further and say that when Indians have to come to Ottawa to present their claims and spend a week or more away from their jobs-or even if they have to spend only two or three days away from their jobs-they should be reimbursed, if they are in full time employment, their daily wage while they are here acting on behalf of their respective bands. Provision should definitely be made for paying the expenses of legal counsel; lawyers should be adequately and properly paid. There should be combined in the provision of adequate payment for legal counsel a provision which will eliminate the excuse which some counsel may find to approach these matters on a contingency basis. I for one would not be too happy if, for example, a $10 million claim was settled in British Columbia and a lawyer collected a 10 per cent contingency fee. Unless very strict control is worked out by the Commission, this is a very real danger.

Indian Claims Commission
I would refer to the suggestion made by the Indian and Eskimo Association in its recommendation to the Minister. They suggested that it might be possible to make grants to the Canadian Bar Association, to be administered by it, to assist the preparation of claims. They suggested also that it might be desirable for the Canadian Bar Association to set forth for its members rules of ethical conduct in connection with Indian claims where the present rules might be thought to lack clear guidance. I think it would be highly desirable for the Commission to work out some sort of arrangement with the Canadian Bar Association to prevent a situation arising whereby a lawyer who collected a $10 million claim, let us say, on behalf of an Indian band would be paid a huge contingency fee. I would not be too happy with a result like that, and I do not think any Member of this House would be.
I hope the Government will grant to every Indian band which has a claim adequate time in which to present that claim. The two-year period in Bill No. C-130 certainly was inadequate, and I hope the proposed bill will contain a provision for a longer claim period. Once the bill is passed I hope the Department of Indian Affairs will contact and recontact every Indian band in this country which has a possible claim, so that these claims will be made within a reasonable period and without too much delay. I believe the administration should work out a system whereby perhaps at three-monthly intervals notice would be sent to every band in the country, because I feel it is most important and it will be easier in the long run for the ministry if we can get all these claims in now, and not be faced two or three years from now with demands for an extension of the period for claims.
I hope that the bill will set forth clearly that the normal rules of evidence shall not be strictly enforced with regard to claims presented to the Commission. If we applied the normal rules of evidence strictly we would find that a host of possible claims would be ineligible. Custom and tradition should be taken into consideration in support of evidence. I believe this Commission must be instructed to be flexible. A lot will depend upon the selection of the Chairman of the Commission, but it is most important that the Chairman should consider his job as being one to assist in satisfying Indian claims if at all possible. He should not approach his job in any sense of acting on behalf of the Gov-
June 21, 1965

Canada. I am confident, and I am sure it is the hope of every hon. Member here, that the Commission will contribute toward purging from our midst this unfortunate past which continues to impede the progress of our Indian population. I hope that when the Department contacts individual bands requesting that claims be forwarded, this particular point will be stressed and that the emphasis will be on the future. I hope this measure, in comparison with the most important measures of community development and education, will not obscure what is the objective of this Government, and I think of every Member of this House, namely a better life for all our Indians with full participation in our national wealth.

Mr. Chairman, I can assure you that what I have to say this evening will be very brief, because all I can do is endorse what has been said by the speakers who have preceded me, and also congratulate the Minister for finally bringing in this resolution, the implementation of which will provide for the Indian people that long awaited Indian Claims Commission.
This is not an argumentative subject, Mr. Chairman. Everyone is interested in the welfare of the Indian people. It is my privilege to represent 7,000 of them in my constituency. I have watched these Indian people develop over the years, and this has been an extremely interesting experience. In my opinion these people have a great potential, which has been shown on many occasions. There has been a steady improvement in British Columbia, where we now have 90 per cent of the Indian children going to school. I think that probably this is the greatest step we can undertake to improve the status of the Indian in our country.
Indian claims, of course, date back to the coming of the white man. In British Columbia they would date back at least 160 years, so this is nothing new. Their rights have been abused, there is no argument about that. Some of this has been intentional, some of it unintentional. I feel that when this bill is introduced it should have terms of reference for the Commission which will be extremely broad. This bill should be for the general welfare of the Indian, rather than just establishing a Claims Commission to settle land rights. It can do a great deal to improve the lot of Indians throughout the country. I feel its terms of reference should include the improvement of their educational advantages, I feel they should be allowed economic advice. I

Indian Claims Commission feel they should have agricultural assistance and that we should encourage industry among these Indian people. Many could undertake industry on their lands, which at the present time are lying dormant. I am thinking particularly of the fact that some of these areas are rich in timber interests. Something should be done to encourage these Indians to develop their own timber rights. At the present time these areas are undeveloped or are being used by outside private interests.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
We must protect the Indians' hunting and fishing rights. These things should all be included in the bill to be brought down. We must assist these Indians to help themselves to become independent citizens in our communities. If we do this, these people will be a great advantage to our general economy.
Their land rights are going to be difficult to define and settle and undoubtedly this Commission will run into many problems. I can foresee that many of these claims to land! on the part of Indians will actually not be submitted in writing. Many of these treaties date back to the time when Indians could not read or write. Many of these Indians who have claims to lands today still cannot read or write. Under the circumstances it would be a very serious mistake to insist that the Indians present their claims in writing. That is what happened in respect of the bill that was brought into this House in December of 1963. It stated that the Indians should present their claims in writing and, of course, in most cases that was impossible. We must see that the Indians have good legal advice, and I feel that affidavits should be acceptable to the Commission. If we are to deal fairly with the Indians affidavits should be considered as being adequate proof of claims. These claims should be supported in the form of affidavits rather than by writing in a language which the Indian does not understand.
We must give the benefit of the doubt to the Indian people. Many of them are honest in their claims, and in most cases I know they are justified in claiming rights to lands. They should be protected and given the benefit of the doubt when their claims are being considered. I look forward to this bill being presented. I have every confidence that the Minister will introduce a Bill which will be acceptable to all parties and, what is more important, to the Indian people throughout Canada. I hope we will be able to accept the bill without prolonged dispute. I am sure

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks because of my interest in this subject.
Make them short.

this claim. The lands which are claimed by the Six Nations now are not in the possession of the Crown. They belong to other parties, and have belonged for many years, and it comes to this simply, that if this land belongs to the Indians and is improperly disposed of, the Province of Ontario must make compensation to these Indians for the value of these lands. Somebody has got to make a compensation for the lands have been sold or disposed of, they cannot be transferred to these Indians, because they belong to other people, and therefore, if the Indians have been wrongfully dispossessed of these lands, of course, they must be compensated either by the Dominion Parliament or the United Province of Canada or the old Province of Upper Canada. We do not know its extent, nor its value, not what was really conveyed, or promised to be conveyed, to the Indians. I feel that the red man should be protected against the white man and against their intrusions upon his rights.
That is to be found in the House of Commons Debates of 1887, pages 207 and 208. This matter was raised again on May 11, 1914, by the hon. Frank Oliver, and as found on page 3537 of Hansard he said:
But there are bands of the Six Nations Indians located on the Grand River in Ontario who, I maintain, are in a different legal position from any Indian bands who are native to the country. These Indian bands on the Grand River had their original home in the United States. At the close of the war of the revolution they emigrated to Canada and were given lands under a special treaty, not as subjects of Great Britain, but as allies of Great Britain, and I maintain that the holding of these Six Nations Indians on the Grand River is of such a kind that this Parliament has no right to interfere with it. I admit that Parliament has the power to interfere with the rights of Indians under treaty made with this Government, but I say that this Parliament has no right to interfere with a treaty made between the Imperial Government and the Six Nations Indians.
I quote these two statements because they indicate that this problem was before the House in 1887 and was again brought to the attention of the House in 1914. It has taken a long time to consider these claims of the Indians and I am very glad to know that this Commission is being appointed for that very purpose. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, with these few brief remarks I wish the Commission every success in all it undertakes to correct any injustices and in so doing lay the foundation for the further improvement and advancement of the native Indians of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to comment briefly in support of the establishment of the Indian Claims Commission. I have the honour to represent an area which embraces Walpole Indian Reserve and I might point out that this reserve is quite far advanced in respect of social services, and so on. Indeed, I believe the Indians there
Indian Claims Commission are unique in Canada inasmuch as recently they have been granted self-government. They are master of their own destiny; they operate their own ship of state. I sometimes wonder if this is not a mixed blessing because there are many things that will have to be straightened out on this reserve. However, I have great confidence that the people there will master the difficulties which will face them in the next few months. I sometimes wonder whether, so far as the Indian Affairs Branch is concerned, the move was a matter of self-preservation from the point of view of getting rid of quite a problem and just letting the Indians operate on their own, or whether it was actually done for the advancement of the people. I prefer to think that the latter was the reason.
I have no hesitation in supporting the establishment of the Commission because I feel we owe so much to these people, particularly in my part of the country, who were our allies and friends in days gone by in the developing of this great country. Indeed, the death of that great general and ally, Chief Tecumseh, took place in my area and he is buried there somewhere. We are not just sure where, but he is there some place.
In the establishment of this Commission I hope the Government will be sincere and that the Indian people will not be led down the garden path of great political promises. At the same time I would caution the Indian people not to try to embarrass the Government with frivolous claims. I support the principle of the establishment of the Indians Claims Commission because I feel it is something that is long overdue.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about this legislation because within the limits of my constituency, I have an Indian reservation of which I am very proud indeed. I am proud of their accomplishments because they have taken a keen interest not only in their own affairs but also in the affairs of the community as a whole. I am naturally interested in this legislation and more particularly so because I am Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister who is introducing the legislation.
The general principle of the legislation under discussion and the reasons for establishing the Indian Claims Commission are to be commended by all Canadians. This is an important step toward the implementation of the Government's desire to do all it can to give the Indian people every op-
June 21, 1965

Indian Claims Commission portunity to secure their just rights. I dare say that the Commission will hear and make recommendations with respect to a broad category of Indian claims. Indian bands or groups will be able to put forward claims, which may very well go back in time, regarding loss of lands that were reserved for Indians and for which no compensation was paid to them, the failure to discharge treaty obligations, or the improper use of band funds and generally any transactions that have taken place that may be said to have caused injury to the Indians because of the failure of the Crown to act fairly or honourably with the Indians.
The Minister's interest in the welfare of the Indian people is reflected by his being the first Minister, to my knowledge to appoint a full blooded Indian to his staff as a special assistant. As pointed out by the Minister, band councils and Indian delegations were consulted after the introduction of Bill C-130 and this has resulted in changes which are going to be incorporated in the new bill. The purpose of the legislation is to hear and determine claims of Indians and it is intended that such a Commission should be independent and have a degree of permanency.
This afternoon and evening we have heard quite a number of worth-while contributions from hon. Members in all parties in the House, and I urge every Member to support the resolution moved by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. This legislation means the acceptance of a legal and moral obligation by the Government of Canada to assure that Indians can have their day in court. Persons interested in the welfare of Indians will be happy to know that a start is being made toward the establishment of impartial hearings form claims, with the object in view that before more of the early Indians pass on to their reward redress for any injustices will be made.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, may I add just a brief word to this debate. I should like to associate myself with the other Members who have joined in welcoming this legislation to set up an Indian Claims Commission. The Indians of Canada have looked forward for several years now to the establishment of this Commission. As one of those who sat on the Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons for several years, I feel that this is possibly the most useful recommendation that resulted from the deliberations of that Committee. I believe from what the
Indians told us during the hearings of the Committee they have always felt a considerable degree of disappointment and frustration in the way they have been treated by the Canadian Government and the Canadian people, for better than 100 years. They accepted in good faith these agreements that were made with the various sovereigns of Britain. These agreements were to run as long as the sun shone and the waters flowed. They were accepted in good faith and in simple terms.
The Indians did not understand legal terminology or the finer points of business contracts. I should like to support wholeheartedly the remarks that were made by the hon. Member for Peace River as he described how the Indians may have cause for complaint as a result of their lack of business experience and understanding of the law. I can understand their disappointment and feeling of frustration at the way these contracts have been honoured by the Canadian Government and the Canadian people.
I am glad that the Government has seen fit to put in the notice of a resolution on the order paper, item No. 4, indicating their intention to provide assistance to Indian bands in preparing and presenting claims. I hope that the Government will see fit to be really generous in this regard. I suggest that, in so far as possible, the Indian people themselves should be permitted to choose their own counsel, and the Government should be prepared to pay the cost of such counsel. I feel that this is the only way in which the Indians could really have a feeling of satisfaction and fulfilment in connection with the matters to be considered by the Indian Claims Commission. These matters are very complex, very far reaching. There is the matter of their hunting privileges, which they have always understood would never be taken away from them. However, as the hon. Member for Peace River pointed out, the Government of Canada has seen fit to make agreements and laws, such as the Migratory Birds Convention Act, which transgress the original contracts into which the Indian people entered. There is the matter of the Jay Treaty which the Indians still claim gives them the right to cross the border between the United States and Canada freely, without let or hindrance.
These things should be settled, and if possible a full explanation should be offered to the Indians so they will have a clear understanding, if their claims cannot be met, why they cannot be met. I hope that out of the work of this Indian Claims Commission the

June 21, 1965

Indians will find a feeling of satisfaction. If their claims cannot be met they will have a full understanding of why they cannot be met. I hope some of the claims can be met.
I hope that the feeling of frustration the Indians have with regard to the way they have been treated will have disappeared as a result of the work of this Indian Claims Commission, and that the Indians will have their confidence restored in the Canadian Government and the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, it seems as though this is one of those rare occasions upon which unanimity is reached on issues that are brought before the Committee. I appreciate the opportunity of listening to all the representations that have been made in the course of this discussion today. It seems quite a long time ago that I first heard discussions relative to the subject of an Indian Claims Commission. It has been discussed at some length in the House on various occasions. It has even found its way on to the order paper in the form of a private bill, as well as a Government order. Now it seems as though we have reached the point where something is going to be done to implement this recommendation to set up an Indian Claims Commission. Today we are certainly giving our wholehearted support to the resolution that is now before us.
I remember the measure that was introduced last year and the criticism with which it was met. Many suggestions were made and many amendments were proposed. Of course we do not know to what extent the Government has acceded to the requests for amendments or how many of them will find their way into this new measure. I had the opportunity of spending some time at an Indian conference in my own constituency just a short time ago. The question was raised as to whether or not a further opportunity was going to be given to study this bill before it was finally passed in the House. The Indian people at that convention felt it would be advisable, following second reading, for the bill to be given wide publicity and then adequate time elapse so the Indian organizations and the Indian people who are concerned about Indian problems would have an opportunity to make further recommendations and suggestions.
I raised this question some time ago in the House and I was not too sure of the significance of the answer. The Minister seemed to imply that this would not be done, that the amendments were now being considered and

Indian Claims Commission the bill would be carried through once we commenced these discussions. I do not know if I misunderstood him, but I just wanted to make it clear the Indian people feel they should have a further opportunity to study this measure before it is finally passed.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
I shall not enumerate all the amendments that were suggested, but there are two I want to mention. It seems that the Indian people do not feel there should be a time limit on the registration of claims. In fact they feel the Commission should more or less be a permanent one, qualified to deal with claims that may arise from time to time down through the years. No doubt the Minister has given this careful, detailed study.
Another matter which is of great concern to the Indians is the rules of evidence that will be applied in submitting and processing claims. The Indian people will not be able to follow the customary rules in this respect because in many cases they do not have written documents, and their claims are based on what has been handed down to them through generations by word of mouth.
I agree with the hon. Member for Kamloops who said the Indian people should be given the benefit of the doubt in every circumstance.
The Indian people are desirous of offering suggestions and making recommendations on their own. The question was raised by them, "Are we going to accept just what the Government thinks is good for us, what the nonIndian thinks is good for us, or are we to have the opportunity to present our own views and have them implemented?" They understand their own problems best and can offer solutions for them.
During the debate my mind went back to previous references to charters. There is the workmen's charter and the veterans' charter. Would it not be a good thing to provide an Indian charter that would ensure the rights and prerogatives of the Indian people in this great country of ours?
Just recently it was revealed in Saskatchewan that some Indians had been deprived of certain rights in the health field, and the question was raised that there may be other instances of Indians having lost their rights because old treaties have been forgotten. There is growing concern over the needs of the Indian people in Canada. This is true with respect to Government, with respect to Parliament and with respect to the Canadian people as a whole, and I look forward to the

Indian Claims Commission time when Indian people themselves will feel that everything possible has been done to assure them of their rights and privileges as the first citizens of this great country.

Before the resolution carries I think it is important at this juncture to see if we can get some formal indication from the Government as to the timetable, if any, it may have in mind with respect to the proposed Committee.
I would like to ask the Minister whether the government has any desire regarding the speed at which the Committee should meet? Does it have any timetable or anticipation of how long it might be before the Committee could conclude its hearings? Does it have any desire to establish a Commission within a certain period of time? Does it have any intention to circulate the bill to all Indian bands and organizations in Canada, as was done with Bill No. C-130, and does it have any intention to allow a period of time to lapse between the introduction of the bill and the commencement of Committee hearings, in order to give native Indian people the opportunity fully to examine the bill and be prepared as best they can to present their ideas about it to the committee?

Mr. Chairman, since we cannot get second reading of the bill without unanimous consent today, it would be my hope that we could get second reading tomorrow, and following second reading I propose to introduce a resolution proposing the appointment of a Joint Committee of both Houses of Parliament to consider the bill. Of course, we can only do our part here in that regard, and then refer it for sympathetic consideration to the other place. Perhaps I may be speaking out of turn but I propose to suggest that the membership of the committee be 14 from the House of Commons and say 10 from the other place.
If the bill gets second reading tomorrow, as I hope it will, then the Whips of the different parties could get together and nominate their respective Members within a matter of a few days.
I do not think the Government should instruct the Joint Committee of both Houses as to how it should function, but I hope it will organize itself fairly quickly. I have advised representatives of the Six Nations Indians that they will be given an opportunity to appear before the Committee, if the Committee itself agrees-as I certainly expect it will. If the Committee wants to send out copies of the bill to others that can be done.

I would point out that we are all hoping we can get away for a break in the not too distant future, and I would expect distribution of copies of the bill could take place before we recess for the summer. There should then be ample time for the Indian people and others concerned to study the bill and put forward or make such representations to the Committee as they see fit.

That answers one question, at least from the Government's point of view, but I had rather hoped the Government would delay progress on the Committee until the fall. We do not need the Committee simply to organize itself, think about the distribution of the bill, and then wait until the fall. Distribution of the bill could take place without formal organization of the Committee. The Indian Affairs Branch has all the addresses and names on addressograph plates, and could very easily send the bill out, without leaving it to the doubtful operation of a Committee as to the speed with which it wants to proceed.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
I for one say it would be grossly unfair for Parliament, for a committee, for any part of Parliament or of the Senate, to proceed with speed in considering this matter, especially so far as the west coast Indian people are concerned. As the Minister well knows, they are just now embarking on the salmon fishing season, and the people there whose livelihood rests on the fishing industry will not have the time or the opportunity to study the bill carefully until some time in the fall. If there is any speed or any desire to rush this thing through at this juncture, it will simply mean, so far as the B.C. people are concerned, that they will be denied the opportunity to examine the bill fully. It would be my suggestion that the Minister might, as a matter of Government policy, simply say that it is the intention of the Government to distribute this bill to all Indian bands in Canada, all interested organizations and everybody who sent in briefs about Bill No. C-130, with an indication that the Committee will meet some time in the fall. He could make that declaration very simply.

Mr. Chairman, I would hope that the Committee could meet within the next week or ten days. If there is any chance of delay in the Committee meeting because of delay in the nominations to be made in the two Houses, then I can assure hon. Members that steps will be taken along the lines of those taken following the introduction of the bill in December, 1963, to
June 21. 1965	COMMONS
see that suitable publicity is given. There is no intention to rush this bill through without giving all interested parties the opportunity to come here and discuss it in the light of the changes that we have made or put forward.
On second reading, which I hope will be tomorrow, I will deal with the several suggestions that have been put forward today.
I cannot do it properly until the bill has been made public. If for any reason this Committee should not be set up and be functioning within the next week or ten days, then the hearings could be fixed for such time in the fall as the Committee sees fit to determine.

Mr. Chairman, there is a suggestion I am going to throw out to the Minister that he might consider between now and the time the Committee is finally established after the other place has completed its deliberations and has given the bill second reading. We discovered during the course of the joint committee hearings that a considerable amount of delay was occasioned because of the difficulty made by various Indian people throughout the country.
I do not know what the view of the Government is with regard to this, but I know they have had representations made both orally and through letters and briefs. I assume the establishment of a Committee means that they are prepared as well to entertain representations from others appearing before the Committee, particularly of course from the Indian peoples and different bands. The Government might give consideration to including in the terms of reference the right for the Committee to adjourn from place to place. This might well expedite the hearings. I doubt whether the expense involved would be any more than the expense in connection with bringing to Ottawa from a number of areas the different witnesses who were heard before the Committee. I am not necessarily wedded to that idea, Mr. Chairman, but I have put it out for the Minister's consideration.
I was going to bring to the Minister's attention some questions that I and other hon. Members had put forward, but I take it from his answer to the hon. Member for Skeena that it is his intention when introducing the bill and asking for second reading to deal in more detail with the questions and suggestions which have been put forward, so we can relate them to the terms of the bill which will then be available. If this

Indian Claims Commission is the case I do not intend to pursue my questions at this time.
I also suggest to the Minister that in order to expedite second reading the Minister might indicate that the Government is not wedded too firmly to the terms of the bill as it is introduced and that they are prepared, within the limits of their responsibility as a Government, to go along with and not oppose views brought forward by the Committee and brought to the attention of the Government following the Committee hearings. It may be that the terms of the legislation as presented tomorrow may be acceptable in toto, but I am inclined to think that there will probably be some suggestions made as to change. that the House go into Committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize and to provide for the construction of a line of railway in the Province of Ontario by Canadian National Railway Company from a point of the Froomfield Spur near Sarnia in a southerly direction for a distance of approximately twelve miles to the property of Canadian Industries Limited in Sombra Township in the County of Lambton at a total estimated expenditure of $850,000, not to be exceeded by more than fifteen per cent.

subtopic: MEASURE TO AUTHORIZE CONSTRUCTION OF SPUR LINE TO CANADIAN INDUSTRIES LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this resolution is to authorize the Canadian National Railway Company to construct out of funds within the railway company and out of their present capital budget a line of railway approximately 12 miles long running from a point commencing at mile 32 of the Canadian National Froomfield spur, extending in a southerly direction for a distance of about 12 miles to the property of Canadian Industries Limited in Sombra Township, in the County of Lambton, Province of Ontario. The estimated cost of the rail spur will be $850,000, which is the amount provided for, plus a 15 per cent provision for contingencies.
The Canadian National Railways have carried out an economic study of this particular branch line, which is designed to join the new plant of Canadian Industries Limited with the main line. The company has decided that it is an economically feasible branch line and will pay for itself within a reasonably short period of time.

The purpose of this Canadian Industries plant is the production of fertilizer. It is estimated that 400,000 tons of fertilizer per annum will be produced by this particular plant, and approximately 225,000 will pass over this branch line. The method of financing the construction, as I have mentioned, is out of the existing capital budget of the Canadian National Railways, so that this House will not be asked to vote additional funds for this purpose but merely to allow the Canadian National Railways to proceed with the construction of this new branch line.

subtopic: MEASURE TO AUTHORIZE CONSTRUCTION OF SPUR LINE TO CANADIAN INDUSTRIES LIMITED

It would be very helpful if the Canadian National Railways had authority to proceed with this line in order that the construction materials for this plant could be hauled over the railway, thus providing additional revenues for the railway and also providing facilities for the manufacturers.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure we are all interested in the fact that the Canadian National Railways are interested in building this new spur line in western Ontario. To me this pinpoints two factors: First, that the tremendous development that has taken place, which began in 1961 in the Province of Ontario and the whole Dominion of Canada, is continuing. After all, the Canadian National Railways, as the Minister of National Revenue has indicated, made an economic study and found that this branch line was economically feasible.
It also pinpoints the fact that branch lines are important in this tremendous development which we are passing through today. In the first place, Canadian Industries Limited, which is not a new company in Canada, realize that the railroad is important. Regardless of the fact that the plant they are thinking of building is served by some of the best highways in Ontario, and that the plant
June 21, 1965	COMMONS
is not too far away from good lake ports with access to the facilities of the St. Lawrence Seaway, which provides cheap and economic transportation, they also feel that the railroad branch lines are important to their continued development.
The second matter I should like to speak about concerns the importance of branch lines themselves. A tremendous study of transportation was made by the MacPherson Commission, which dealt extensively with the subject of branch lines. Much talk has been heard these days of a reduction in the number of branch lines, but I feel that the resolution before us pinpoints, as I say, the importance of branch lines as well as the importance of maintaining and preserving most of the present branch lines a fact which I feel the Government should stress to Canadian National Railways.
Representing as I do an area in western Ontario where there are many rumours and much talk of discontinuing branch lines, and having read the report of the Economic Council which indicates that our population and gross national product are going to increase, I feel that before there is any discontinuance of branch lines or downgrading of service Canadian National Railways or the Government should give very thorough consideration to the possibility that in this area new industry might like to develop. We are told our population will increase so that additional transportation facilities will be necessary.
As I say, in the area in which I live there is a lot of worry in small communities, towns and villages over the prospect that railways might be taken away and that some of the branch lines might be discontinued. But I feel that this particular resolution now before us indicates the importance of the railways to our economic development. There is not a community in my riding which is not worrying about ways and means of getting additional industry. That the Government is interested in this is indicated by the statement made by the Prime Minister on June 7, one paragraph of which I should like to read, because I think it is very important. As recorded at page 2023 of Hansard the Prime Minister said:
With this objective we propose to establish new guide lines for the designation of areas where, under the terms of the Department of Industry Act, the industrial incentives will be made available.
We have heard a lot about designated areas and assistance which is going to be given

Canadian National Railways to industry, but I feel that there are other areas in which assistance can be given to industry. In underdeveloped areas and areas where there is a crying need for industry the municipalities should be assisted by means of industrialized assessments to meet the tax rate in order to provide the schools, hospitals and roads and all the things required by a small community, just the same as in a large community. I feel that the Government should carry this proposal regarding the development of industry further afield into the area of assisting the means of transportation through some type of subsidy in order to facilitate the settlement of industry in such areas. After all, industry needs raw materials and components. This would be of great benefit to the smaller communities all throughout Ontario and Canada.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)

Irrespective of the fact that this involves a branch line costing $850,000 to assist Canadian Industries Limited to get their fertilizer to the markets, this is an indication of the necessity of maintaining branch lines, and probably an indication of the necessity to build more. speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (for the Minister of Finance) moved
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill C-119, to amend the Customs Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the time of the resolution covering this particular bill I explained the contents of the legislation very thoroughly, I think, and we had a rather thorough discussion of those contents. However, there are one or two points which arose during the discussion at the resolution stage and I should like to comment very briefly on them. One of them had to do with the proposed amendment introducing a new section 37A of the Customs Act whose purpose is to assist Great Britain and other compact countries in the sale of their products to Canada by adopting a means of alleviating some of the difficulties which arise in determining the cost of their goods for distribution in Canada, compared with goods coming from other countries which have a similar system of distribution to that used in Canada.
One of the points raised during the debate on the resolution by the hon. Member for Edmonton West was the matter of so-called ministerial discretion included in this particular section and which I should like to point out to him is not ministerial discretion but discretion of the Governor in Council. He tried very hard to compare this provision with a situation which arose a few years ago in which ministerial discretion was being introduced into the Customs Tariff Act and

June 21, 1965
Customs Act
legislation brought in by the former government was subsequently refused passage by the Senate.
I should like to point out that there is a great deal of difference between the legislation now being introduced in the House of Commons and the legislation to which my hon. friend alluded. First of all, the amendments which were introduced at that time had to do with the matter of class or kind rulings in Canada. It was proposed that the Minister be given the right to rule whether or not something was of a class or kind in Canada even though such goods had never been produced in this country. In other words, it was proposed at that time that the Minister would be given the right to rule something was of a class or kind made in Canada if production facilities existed, even though the item had never been produced in this country.
Ruling something to be of a class or kind made in Canada has two implications. First of all, if it is within one of the tariff items that has a class or kind condition attached to it a higher customs duty attaches to the item.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The other, and more important part, is that if it is ruled of a class or kind made in Canada, even though class or kind is not mentioned in the particular tariff item, then dumping duties are applicable. For example, there is no reference to class or kind in Section 438(a) covering autos. If the Minister of National Revenue, under legislation to which my hon. friend alluded, if that legislation had been passed, had ruled that these were of a class or kind made in Canada, dumping duties could have been employed even though there is no mention of class or kind in that particular item.
Now, I should like to mention that there are various methods by which the value for duty, already established under Order in Council, may be appealed under the proposed new Section 37A. First, there are the same rights of appeal to the Tariff Board and Exchequer Court as exist with regard to imports as prescribed in the Customs Act under Sections 43, 44 and 45. I will remind my hon. friend that in 1962 they changed Section 43 of the Customs Act by extending the period under which an appeal could be made to the Chief Appraiser. At that time, they did not take the point of view that it did not matter whether or not such an appraisal was made. A Canadian manufacturer who, under this proposed section felt that an importer was securing a value for duty under

this provision below the cost of production plus an allowance for gros profit, could appeal under existing appeal provisions. Similarly, an importer could use existing appeal provisions if he felt that the regular valuation of his goods, from which a reduction was being made under this section was too high.
The Canadian manufacturer similarly could appeal that such regular valuation, before the reduction was made, was too low. The Canadian manufacturer, if it were not feasible to use the regular appeal procedures under Sections 43, 44 and 45, could request the Deputy Minister to refer the matter of valuation to the Tariff Board under Section 46 of the Customs Act. The importer has a similar right of appeal. Finally, action by the Governor in Council is subject to appeal to the Exchequer Court on the ground that the discretion to reduce the value for duty has been recognized unreasonably. It is clear, therefore, that under this proposed section there will be the same significant rights of appeal both for the importer and for the Canadian producer to the Tariff Board and to the courts.
However, Mr. Speaker, the point I should like to make to the House is that the whole intention of Section 37A, which is being introduced into the Customs Act is to assist compact countries such as Britain in their exports to this country. While it is true that under Section 22 of the Financial Administration Act, the Governor in Council can alleviate the duties in various situations which might arise, or almost any situation if it were deemed advisable to do so, it was felt by the Government, on the urging of the British Government, that it would be more useful to write into the Customs Act a specific provision such as Section 37A which would allow the Governor in Council to use the Customs Act for alleviating the duty burden, or the unfair burden as the British have often called it, which their goods must bear rather than having to use Section 22 of the Financial Administration Act.

From the Minister's brief remarks with regard to Bill No. C-72 of 1961 it is rather apparent that the Minister, who was not then in the House, is not seized of the full import of what was being attempted at the time. I think if he consulted the debates of the day he would have found that what was being attempted at that time was precisely what is being done now, to incorporate into the legislation some-
June 21, 1965

thing which had existed by Order in Council. This business of class or kind was not something new. It had existed prior to 1936. In fact, the percentage of Canadian consumption of 10 per cent was something fixed by Order in Council in 1936. These provisions were being substantially incorporated into the Statute in 1961.
However, the point I was after was one which dealt more with the objections that were made by the Opposition of the day. Primarily, what they said was there was a denial of the right of appeal. I maintain that under Section 37A there is no true right of appeal. One can say that there are rights of appeal. However, let us examine them, and then we will see whether there are really the rights of appeal the Minister has indicated. A decision by the Governor in Council on a report by the Minister, as envisaged by Section 37A, is not a decision that the Dominion Customs Appraiser will set aside, nor will the Deputy Minister who, after all, had a great deal to do with the preparation of the report of the Minister. Certainly, we are not going to get a divided House in the Department of National Revenue. Therefore, I fail to see how, in essence, a Deputy Minister could still maintain his decision and grant an appeal to any interested party with regard to a reduction in valuation as envisaged under Section 37A.
Certainly we know that Section 37A has in mind, as its objective, really exercising a form of discrimination in favour of a certain country or countries. Conversely, I suppose we might say there is discrimination against others. Here is a specific valuation that is being set up for the reduction that is recommended by the Governor in Council, and as I indicated I do not believe the appeal to the Dominion Customs Appraiser is a true appeal. Neither is it a true appeal to the Deputy Minister. The Act would allow an appeal to the Tariff Board; that is so. However, when we come to the appeal to the Exchequer Court, the Minister must take cognizance of the wording of Section 45, wherein it is stated clearly that the appeal to the Exchequer Court of Canada relates to any question of law. Certainly, the Minister is not going to argue that the Exchequer Court is going to say that the reduction in value was unreasonable; that is a matter of discretion, not a question of law. [DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
The only point of law, I would submit, would be if the Government moved in some fashion procedurally contrary to the pro-
Customs Act
visions of the Act. But no court will substitute its discretion for that of a Minister acting within the letter of the law, nor of the Governor in Council acting according to the letter of the law. The Minister knows this, and it is my contention that there is very little room for appeal, if any, in this instance.
I can compare what is being done now with the outcry that was raised by some of the Minister's former colleagues, and some of his present colleagues, when they sat on this side of the House. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) and the former Minister of Justice were like the Bobsey Twins on that occasion. The debate lasted for nine days.
Sometimes hon. Members opposite wonder about legislation taking a long time to pass, but on that occasion an amendment, much the same length as this one, was discussed for nine days. Was that filibuster?
Oh, no.
Was that obstruction?
Oh, no.

They were not accused of it. The Government of the day said hon. Members were exercising their right to object and it may be that, except for administrative reasons, there was some right to object. If the Minister reads Bill C-72 I am sure he will agree with me that if the duty were to evolve upon him to determine a classification of a class or kind, it would be much easier to proceed under Bill C-72 as then proposed. The Minister cannot deny this, yet we had that great outcry. Why, it was almost a traducing of Magna Carta, hon. Members were so indignant on that occasion.
Why is there this sudden change? I am not complaining about discretion within the Act, because both under the Customs Act and the Customs Tariff Act the Minister possesses all sorts of discretion. As I indicated the other day, the counting shows there are over 60 areas in which the Minister may exercise his discretion. Introducing a further discretion at this time does not unduly worry me. What concerns me is that we are told this is subject to appeal, which I say is not a true appeal.
I shall not bore the House by reading passages from the previous debate to which I refer, but the hon. Member for Laurier of that day, and the Minister of Transport, figured prominently in it, and I think the Minister should read that debate.

June 21, 1965
Customs Act
I did.

Then I hope he was educated as to how attitudes can change. It depends on what side of the House you may be on. I can only say that a lot of the protestations of that day must have been hollow. In so far as the former hon. Member for Laurier was concerned, there was a little bit of in-fighting. Mr. Deputy Speaker is the hon. Member representing Cornwall and he knows whereof I speak. There was a good deal of confusion and difficulty with regard to the textile industry in Cornwall; but let it be known that today, as a result of action taken by the administration of a few years ago, the level of activity in the textile industry is much healthier than it was in 1957 and 1958, when plants were closing.
I wonder what the textile industry may have to say if the Government is to exercise its discretion under Section 37A with regard to textiles. After all, automobiles are not the only area in which the British government has expressed its concern about Canada's anti-dumping legislation. Anti-dumping legislation is not new in this country, and certainly it was invoked in regard to textiles. Is it going to be invoked again, or is the Minister going to exercise the prerogatives of Government under Section 37A to let in British textiles to the detriment of the Canadian textile industry? This is a question which the Government will have to determine. The provision is not limited to automobiles. It covers all sorts of categories of goods, and we will see the reactions of industry in regard to these provisions.
The methods of marketing in Great Britain are different from what they are here, but the point is that Britain is selling to this country. If I may give a personal anecdote, early in the days when I was a prisoner of war we held one of the first commonwealth trade and economic conferences among a body of very informed people who were officers from various commonwealth countries. It was a highly educative and interesting experience.
I remember one old South African colonel who was a very sage man. He had discussed with British manufacturers the marketing of a simple implement, a hoe, among native farmers in South Africa. They preferred to have a red handle on the hoe, but the manufacturers said, "We don't sell our hoes with red handles in Britain and therefore we are not going to send them out with red handles." This simply meant that they would not sell any hoes to South African native farmers. It is
a simple story, but it illustrates what happens in a tightly organized market such as exists in Great Britain and other countries.
If those manufacturers think they are going to sell their goods in this country, where tastes and preferences are different, in the same way as they do in their own country, then of course they will have to take their chances, and if they cannot sell them using their own marketing methods then they will have to change those methods. I do not think the answer lies in a change for valuation purposes There are two sides to this coin.
A lot of the changes proposed are eminently sensible, such as the provision of bond rather than cash. There is the recommendation of the Public Accounts Committee to regularize a practice that was actually in effect, and now this is going to be embodied in the Statute. But I still maintain that section 37A is not as simple as the Government would have us believe.
It can introduce a very dangerous principle into the Act. It does not provide the type of appeal that the Minister would have us believe is there. Therefore I enter this caveat at this time, as I did the other day, and as I shall when we are in Committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. T. Pennell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Bill provides for the implementation, without any change in substance, of the budget resolutions relating to the Customs Tariff which were considered by the Committee of Ways and Means on June 17 and 18. The clauses of the Bill are in the same order as the resolutions, and since there is no change in substance there is very little that I can add at this time that will be of assistance to the House.
Clause 1 provides for the renumbering of the Customs Tariff by Order in Council. Clause 2 provides for the deletion of certain items from the Customs Tariff and the insertion of the items which appear in Schedule A tc the Bill. Clause 3 establishes the new drawback item shown in Schedule B to the Bill. Clause 4 amends item 1220, which appears in Schedule C. Clause 5 provides for the establishment of the item dealing with periodicals, and Clause 6 relates to the coming into force of the previous clauses.

Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary has made it appear rather deceptively simple, but I think there is more to this than he would have us believe at the moment. I am dealing primarily with Schedule D referred to in Clause 5 of the Bill. The other day I did say that I felt this was completely exclusive legislation in that a periodical which transgressed the requirements of the item would be excluded from Canada. I was wondering why a magazine with a split run and which contained more than the maximum permitted percentage of advertising directed to Canadians would be excluded from the country as though it were in the class of pornographic material. It is about in the same category. I hope I am not getting the wrong impression of the legislation, but it seems to me that this is a very heavy penalty.
Customs Tariff
If a publication, whether it be from the United States or from another foreign country, has a split run and contains certain advertising directed to Canadians, why should it be banned from Canada? Is this not a form of censorship? I quite agree with the idea of the Minister, namely to protect Canadian periodicals from the effects of the so-called split run; but surely the remedy is to impose a higher tariff or a fairly punitive customs rate. But at the present time-and I think the Parliamentary Secretary would have to answer this question-why ban the periodical entirely? I cannot quite see that. Certainly the economic impact of a higher customs impost would make it economically impractical to continue to distribute such a magazine in the country. But why ban it?
I hope the Parliamentary Secretary can put me straight, if I am wrong in my estimation of item 1221. I did not think we went quite as far as banning the circulation of such publications-any publications, as a matter of fact-which did not offend morals, were not seditious or did not offend the public interest in a similar way. Why, if there is a split run and there is a non-permitted degree of advertising directed to Canadians, should it be banned? There have been protestations that the Government does not want to impose any form of censorship, but this is censorship; at least in my interpretation of this particular item. With regard to Schedule C, I suppose this would be intended to cover collectors' items. After all, the only change in Item 1220 is in subparagraph (d), which reads:
antique articles eligible for entry under Tariff Item 693(i) or Tariff Item 693(iii), and bona fide collectors' items, as determined by the Minister;

With regard to the rest of the items as enumerated in Schedules A and B, we discussed these at the resolution stage and I will limit my remarks to Item 1221 particularly.
