Mr. Speaker, before the Parliamentary Secretary rises to reply to the hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), and close the debate, I should like to ask, because I am not familiar with this, why there is no specified tariff laid down in schedule D on periodicals, catalogues, newspapers and so on, on which a duty may be imposed. Schedule A and schedule B, for example, contain specific items, and the various rates of duty are also specifically stated.
Bill No. C-120 is asking the House to authorize the Governor in Council to impose by order from time to time amendments and tariffs. I think it is something of a departure to give the Governor in Council the authority, first of all, to impose taxes without the consent of Parliament, and second, a new category of goods is brought in, such as catalogues, newspapers and periodicals. Surely it would be useful to the House, and generally, to know what the Government has in mind by way of tariff rate on these magazines, newspapers and so on.
Another interesting point in this bill is that clause 5 simply says:
Schedule C to the said Act is further amended by inserting therein the item and enumeration of goods specified in schedule D to this Act.
I would ask if schedule D was some kind of afterthought on the part of the Government. Why do we specifically spell out the amendment to Section 17 and itemize the new schedules A, B and C, and then add a further schedule, schedule D, to schedule C? It seems a strange way to write a bill, yet it is what we find in front of us.
If it is not customary for Parliament to grant the Governor in Council the authority to impose tariffs from time to time, such as clause 1 suggests, then I should like to know why it is being done in this manner. If it has been customary in the past for the Minister or the Governor in Council to have this kind of authority which is being asked for here, then this will certainly add to my information.
I was not in the House at the time of the newspaper reports in 1960 and 1961, when the former Government brought in a bill which was going to give the Minister some discretionary power to impose tariffs from time to time on certain classes of goods, but a tremendous amount of objection was taken by the Liberal Party of the day to the effect that passing the bill would in fact give the Minister or the Governor in Council almost what you might call an

executive authority to impose taxes. This is an authority which has been very religiously, if I may use that word, confined to Parliament. First of all, the House of Commons and then the whole parliamentary system are the only bodies with the right to impose taxation. I know of no other instance where a bill has gone through the House transferring this authority to the Governor in Council.
So, Mr. Speaker, when the Parliamentary Secretary replies perhaps he could explain why there is no provision as to the specific rate of tariff which will be imposed, and why the bill is written in such a way that Schedule D is simply added to Schedule C, wherein this power is transferred to the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the Parliamentary Secretary speaks now he will close the debate.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I do not believe it has been the practice that a Parliamentary Secretary is empowered to replace the Minister who moved second reading of the bill. At any time the Parliamentary Secretary has spoken in the past it has been with the unanimous consent of the House. I do not think this is a good practice.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Chair is not establishing the practice now; it has been established before. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Pennell) did not make the motion but spoke on behalf of and for the Minister who made the motion. There is precedent to the effect that the Parliamentary Secretary who has made the originating speech in support of the motion, and who speaks later in reply, closes the debate.
I would refer hon. Members to a ruling by Mr. Speaker Michener, reported in the Journals for Tuesday, May 17, 1960. He said:
I think I should inform the House that if the Parliamentary Secretary speaks now he will close the debate. I do so with a comment, however, because Standing Order 37 refers in express terms only to the honourable Member who has moved a substantive motion. The Parliamentary Secretary did not move this motion. It was moved by a Minister and the Minister spoke as the first speaker but I believe that one of my predecessors has assumed that the Parliamentary Secretary taking part in debate to all intents does so as though he were the mover and would be considered as such for the purpose of closing the debate.
After further debate, the question being put on the said motion, it was agreed to.
I would suggest that the Chair is bound by the previous ruling of Mr. Speaker Michener.

speechtext:
Perhaps it might be of interest Mr. Speaker, to hon. Members, dealing first of all with item 1220, the one dealing with offensive weapons, to note that the amendment to this item has been brought in to make the law applying to those importing firearms the same as the law applying to those who obtain firearms within Canada.
The words "form 42" are deleted from the item so that a person now importing a firearm would do so by using form 43 or form 44. Form 42 was the form which permitted a person to carry a firearm in a place elsewhere than the owner's home or place of business. Form 43 is used to apply for a permit to buy firearms for resale; and form 44 is the application form used for the registering of firearms. I do not know whether this legislation is prompted by the experience in the United States, but on form 42 there is very little provision for description of the firearm. Therefore it would be possible for a person, until this legislation is amended, to take form 42 into the United States, purchase a firearm there and bring it back into Canada, and the firearm in question would not be sufficiently identified, because, as I say, form 42 does not require a detailed description of the firearm. By this amendment we are deleting form 42 and leaving the section requiring only form 43 and form 44. [DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The second amendment will mean that automatic firing military type rifles will be deemed to be a firearm. The other military rifles will continue to come in under subsection (c) as rifles of standard or autoloading type for sporting use only. I think Members should bear in mind the distinction relating to firearms, as I understand it. Under the Criminal Code, firearms include revolvers, pistols, and automatic rifles which continue to fire on a single pressure.
Turning to the somewhat more contentious schedule D, and the suggestion of the hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert)
Customs Tariff
that this might be some type of censorship, and that we should consider dealing with this problem under a higher tariff, let me suggest to him with great respect that it seems to me that his suggestion would be a censorship. We are not aiming at the prohibition of magazines from other countries by schedule D, although it does set up a prohibited list. What we are aiming at by this suggestion is the implementation of a recommendation of the Royal Commission which, and I do not say this in an offensive way, was supported by hon. Members opposite. We are attempting to implement almost verbatim a suggestion of that Royal Commission. What we are doing here is to prohibit magazines if they offend so far as their advertising is concerned.
Split or special editions are usually aimed at capturing the Canadian advertising market, and that is the sort of thing we are aiming to guard against. If a split run, so far as advertising is concerned, is directed primarily at the Canadian market then it will be prohibited. A publisher may adjust his advertising and get around this prohibition. If there had been four editions that have not offended then the fifth edition would be permitted entry into the country. It seems to me that perhaps the tariff items will not have a great effect on the circulation of the type of magazine such as Saturday Evening Post, Harper's and other publications which enjoy wide distribution in Canada and the United States.
Dealing with the point raised by the hon. Member for-

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Parliamentary Secretary a question for clarification? Is schedule D intended to absolutely prohibit the entry into Canada of that type of periodical if it offends under tariff item 1221?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It will be prohibited momentarily, yes, if it offends; but it is open to the publisher to amend the offending advertising and gain readmission. If you read the amendment closely, you will see that any periodical which contains advertising which is primarily directed at the Canadian market but which did not appear in the identical form in all issues of the periodical distributed in the country of origin, then, of course, it would be placed on the prohibited list. I must say, however, that the publishers have been in close contact with the department and are aware of these regulations. We feel they will have no difficulty in meeting the

June 21, 1965
Customs Tariff
requirement and bringing their publications within the exception as set out, in order that they will not be prohibited.
The first part deals only with special editions. Under the second part, in respect of their regular editions, if there is more than 5 per cent of the total advertising space in the magazine used for the purpose of indicating specific sources of availability in Canada, or specific terms or conditions relating to the sale or provision in Canada, of any goods or services, except for the indication of such source of availability or such terms of conditions primarily directed to persons outside Canada, they are prohibited.
The point I want to make, as I suggested in respect of travel magazines, is that the advertising may be about Canada but directed to persons outside Canada, and therefore they will not be prohibited. These are magazines setting out the advantages of visiting Canada and are directed to people outside Canada in an attempt to induce them to come to this country. They would therefore fall within the exceptions and would not be prohibited.
The hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) raised a question, if I understood him correctly, about the method of proceeding by Order in Council. My understanding is, and it will be appreciated that my experience is very limited in this matter, that under Section 10 of the Customs Tariff there may be implementation by Order in Council of certain tariff items. The method being adopted here is one which I think is in keeping with the practice, and is quite proper. All we have done here is state that the prohibited list as set out in schedule D will fall in schedule C, to the Customs Tariff and I cannot think of a more expeditious way of doing this. This is an open move with the intent and purpose being apparent on the face of the clause.

I should like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary a question. When one reads schedule D, 1221 (2), he will see that the first part deals with four immediate preceding issues of a periodical. Is it the intention that the words "at least" should be considered as having been inserted there? What I am getting at is, this is taxing legislation which is construed as striking against the Government. What would be the situation if of the four immediately preceding issues two were offensive in the way in respect of which the Government is trying to prohibit their entry? I am not trying to suggest that there may be a flaw, but in reading this and after listening to the explanations given by 
the Parliamentary Secretary, I cannot decide whether a case could be made for the argument that if two, rather than one, were found to be offensive, and this might be reductio ad absurdum, although plausible, it is admissible.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am satisfied with the wording, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps I should explain that as I understand the clause, if it is found that one publication or issue is offensive then the publisher will have to wait until four consecutive publications are deemed to be inoffensive before the fifth one is admitted. In other words, there have to be four clear publications without any infringement of the item before the fifth is admitted. If there were two publications with infractions, the four issues would be counted from the most recent one, and the fifth would be admitted.

MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations at this time concerning the resolution
DEBATES	2731
Consumer Credit Joint Committee now before the House. In introducing it the Minister said it was self-explanatory, but there is one part he forgot to explain and upon which I should like to enlarge and raise serious objections. I am referring to that part of the resolution reading "and to engage the services of counsel, accountants and such other clerical and technical personnel as may be deemed necessary".
As the Minister said, a Joint Committee on Consumer Credit was set up during the last session and it had its first meeting on June 2,	1964 under the joint chairmanship of
Senator Croll and the hon. Member for Renfrew South. It was my pleasure to be a member of the committee and at its first meeting it was indicated that it was the wish of the committee to hire a lawyer and an accountant to assist. This was something altogether new. To my knowledge I do not know of any other standing committee established by Parliament which has proceeded to hire lawyers, accountants or other professional help.
Objection was raised to this proposal. The matter was discussed in the committee and put to a vote and it was decided that counsel and an accountant would be hired. So the Committee proceeded with professional help. At the first meeting I inquired as to what remuneration these people would receive and these are their rates of pay. Mr. Urie, who was hired as counsel to the committee, was to be paid $250 per day.

speechtext: Shocking.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE

-or for time he spent on the work of the committee over and above attending the committee. The other gentleman, Mr. L'Heureux, was paid on the basis of $100 per day and $20 per hour for preparation time. I think this is outrageous, Mr. Speaker, and I believe the taxpayers of this country are not prepared to pay any such sums.
I object strenuously to the House adopting a resolution with such a provision in it. In my opinion it is outrageous. Let us compare such remuneration with that received by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), for example. If he works 300 days a year he only makes $143 a day compared with this counsel who is being paid $250 a day. If there is any doubt about the outrageousness of these fees, one only needs to ask the hon. Members on the Government side of the House who were mem-
June 21. 1965

Consumer Credit Joint Committee bers of this committee. I think each and every one of them will object to the outrageous fees that have been paid to these two men.
I think they would also agree that their presence had a deteriorating influence on the operations of the committee. When you have a paid official in a committee the members are inclined to say, "Well, why should I take any active part? He is paid $250 a day to do the work. Why should I do any research?" Therefore members do not take the same interest in the committee. There were occasions when matters arose in the committee and the counsel was doing all the speaking. I must say that the accountant hardly ever spoke.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I did not hear him speak during the time I was there. However, there were times when counsel spoke, and he took an altogether different viewpoint from that of the committee. I do not believe this displayed a true picture of the thinking of the committee.
These are some of the objections I have to this clause in this resolution. Now, just to keep the record straight, the committee held 18 meetings during the last session. Mr. Urie completed 170J hours of preparation time and Mr. L'Heureux completed 52J hours of preparation time. The total for counsel amounted to $6,350.55, up to and including February 22. Mr. L'Heureux received $1,855, up to and including the same date. I have therefore, Mr. Speaker, the strongest objection of having this resolution go through in this form. I request the Minister to withdraw that clause and let this committee operate on its own so that any report would be a true expression of the committee. This move would save the taxpayers of this country in the vicinity of $8,200. This is utterly ridiculous, and I am sure there are other Members in the House who would like to support me in this objection.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I was
going to begin by saying that I wanted to commend the Government for bringing forward this resolution. I cannot commend them, however, for bringing forward the resolution at this late date when the House is likely to adjourn within the next couple of weeks and when this House has been meeting now for almost two months. This resolution calls for the reconstitution of the Joint Committee of the House and the Senate to deal with consumer credit. The committee met last year on a number of occasions and was just well into its work when the House adjourned.

Over the years, because there have been so many private Members' bills from all parties in this House attempting to amend the laws of Canada to put some control on the outright robbery which is being perpetrated on the consumers of Canada by various business organizations, this committee was suggested. I am not suggesting for a moment that the vast majority of business organizations in Canada are not legitimate operations. However, there are many organizations coming under federal and provincial jurisdiction that have been fleecing the public high, wide and handsome. It was because of this feeling that Members on all sides felt we should do something, so this committee was set up. I think it is regrettable that the committee has lost two months when it could have been working. The committee has a lot of work to do, many people to hear and many organizations to hear. If it is going to do the job it will have to consult with Provincial Governments.
A number of Provinces, such as the Province of Manitoba from which I come, the Provinces of Ontario and Nova Scotia, as well as others which I cannot think of at the moment, have been looking at the question of consumer credit in great detail. The committee of the Ontario Legislature brought in its report last week and made some very sweeping recommendations. If we are going to do something, Mr. Speaker, to protect the public, then we are going to have to dovetail legislation which will be passed by the Parliament of Canada with legislation that will be passed by the Provinces.
Now, I want to take issue with the Member who just spoke on behalf of the Official Opposition concerning the necessity and the virtue of the committee having expert advice. I agree that the rates at which the accountant and legal counsel were paid sound large. However, this is a separate matter. I think the committee ought to have a good, hard look at that. I served on that committee for a good part of its deliberations. The committee is faced at every meeting with a whole group of expert counsel. I am sure they are paid more than the committee paid the one lawyer and the one accountant who were hired by the committee. The retail credit organizations, the department store organizations all these organizations had their legal counsel there, and they were all there for the definite purpose of trying to convince the committee we ought not to have legislation of this type. They tried to impress upon the committee that fact, that it was impossible, and it would
June 21, 1965

be a disaster-while they did not say for them, that is what they meant-for the committee to recommend and for Parliament to pass legislation which would require the disclosure of the true interest rate. We had a whole series of lawyers and accountants before the committee telling the committee why it should not be done, why it could not be done and why you could not disclose an exact figure for the interest rate.
I want to say, as one who served on that committee, that the committee counsel and accountant served a very useful purpose. I should like to give one small illustration. The accountant was able to develop an exact formula for showing people the exact rate of interest in percentage that they would be paying. The representatives of the financial organizations which appeared before the committee were saying it was impossible to do this. This one statement by the accountant, if that is the only statement he makes for the duration of the committee, will be well worth what he is paid.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The same is true of counsel. The last speaker said this cost the taxpayers of Canada some $8,000. If the committee does a job, if the committee reports to the House on the advisability of such legislation and if the House adopts such legislation, then I submit that the taxpayers of Canada, the consumers of Canada, will save millions of dollars. The expenditure of a few thousand dollars, even if it should be two, three or five times the amount which has already been paid, will be well worth while. I want to say again, as I said when I started discussing this matter, that I am expressing no opinion on the actual amount the committee agreed to pay the lawyer and the accountant. I think that should be looked at. Speaking as a layman who has never been able to earn that amount of money, it sounds a little high to me. However, I say that the principle of hiring expert advisers is a good one which I hope other committees will follow in the future. If they do, then Committees of the House will be able to make reports which will be of value to the House and value to the country as a whole. I hope this joint committee will get going. Before we adjourn for the summer recess, if there is to be one, the steering Committee will be able to map out the next series of witnesses to appear. If there is no recess, I hope the committee will proceed very shortly to finish its work and bring in a report so that Parliament can finally enact

Consumer Credit Joint Committee legislation which is so necessary to protect the buying public.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the re-establishment of the Committee on Consumer Credit. For a long time the public has been concerned about the procedures used in some financial transactions, and is aware of the need for a study into consumer buying. It is unfortunate that so much of the session has gone by before reaching this motion. Valuable time has been lost.
Reference has been made to the committee counsel and accountant, and the suggestion was made that we should not pass the resolution in its present form. However, I do not see anything in it to indicate how much these gentlemen are to be paid. The committee engages its own staff, and therefore I support its re-establishment so that it can get to work immediately.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too support the resolution and agree with others who have said it is unfortunate that the session is so far advanced before re-appointing the Committee. It is a Committee which has a very heavy task, and its work and findings will be followed with great interest by the consuming public, particularly by those who have to resort to credit in order to buy the things they require.
I support the hon. Member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) about the amount paid to counsel. Are we losing all sense of values in our society, paying $250 a day for counsel for a committee like this, and $25 an hour for preparation? Compare that with what a university professor gets, or a farmer, or a skilled workman. People who charge this sort of fee are sucking the blood of our society, and in my opinion are not making a worthwhile contribution.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am glad to see I get some support from the Government benches, including from some of my legal friends. Officials from the staff of the Department of Justice could be used for this purpose.
The hon. Member for Wellington South suggested the resolution should not be adopted because of the fees paid to counsel and accountants, but I agree with the hon. Member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) that we should pass the resolution. It is entirely up to the committee, whom they employ and the amount they are willing to pay; but I trust the
2734	COMMONS
Consumer Credit Joint Committee committee will take note of what has been said in this debate.
Turning to the question of accountants, in my experience accountants are very necessary in the society in which we live. They are the ones who do the exact thinking, who make the precise decision which can be of great interest to all persons, particularly those who have to pay income tax and things like that. Accountants play an important role in our society and, as pointed out by the hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), one of the accountants who appeared before the committee-in passing, they are not paid nearly as much as members of the legal profession-made an important submission which might save a great deal for the Canadian consumer.
Before resuming my seat, once again I protest the exorbitant fees paid to counsel in Canada because I think they are entirely unnecessary in relation to the services they perform in our society.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think we should rush passage of this resolution, for two good reasons. It has been brought forward as a filler because we completed the list of items the Government had placed before us, which shows our anxiety to cooperate and get on with the business. It would appear as if the Government were not ready to go ahead with something it could announce a day or a week before.
The second reason is that suggestions have been given tonight which would warrant second thoughts by the Government with regard to the resolution. Important as it is to reconstitute the committee, the session is possibly drawing to a close. The other House does not appear to be meeting. I do not hear any faint noises from the other part of the Parliament buildings and it might not be possible to get the committee set up quickly.
Objections have been expressed to the committee appointing its own counsel and accountants. These are valid objections. The competent Civil Service that Canada possesses should be able to provide all the skilled personnel required for this type of work, whether from the Department of Justice, the Department of Trade and Commerce or the Department of Industry. I could name half a dozen members of the Civil Service

who would give competent advice and assistance to the committee without the employment of outside assistance.
May I call it ten o'clock.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING INSTRUCTIONS IN WIRE TAPPING
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING INSTRUCTIONS IN WIRE TAPPING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to discuss the answer which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) gave to a question of mine last week in respect of the use by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police of wire tapping and electronic equipment. The Minister's statement was very clear; when you strip away the legal phraseology, the Minister said in effect that the R.C.M.P. does not carry on wire tapping in this country.
I do not believe that the Minister of Justice would knowingly misinform the House of Commons. I must therefore believe, on the basis of evidence I have, that the R.C.M.P. is not telling the Minister of Justice the real facts of what goes on in this country. I want to deal tonight, because my time is very limited, with only one illustration. On February 13, 1965, the Toronto Globe and Mail carried a story the headline of which was "Wiretap Set Up for Lamontagne-Rouleau Call: R.C.M.P. Officer". The story is dated Ottawa and the first paragraph says:
An inspector of the R.C.M.P. told the Dorion inquiry yesterday that arrangements were made last August to tap a telephone conversation between Pierre Lamontagne and Guy Rouleau, then Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister Lester Pearson.
I am not here to defend Mr. Rouleau but I think, like an American Supreme Court Justice, that wire tapping is a dirty business and ought to be prohibited. I also think the Minister of Justice should tell the House what really goes on. I asked the question about this after that news story appeared, and the answer I got was that the R.C.M.P. did not and does not tap wires in order to listen in to telephone conversations. So after a great deal of difficulty I got a transcript of the hearings of the Dorion Commission of February 12, 1965, and I want to put on the record in the few minutes available to me the exchange 22620-174
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion of questions by one of the counsel, Paul Jolin, and the answers given by Inspector J. R. R. Carriere of the R.C.M.P. I will give the page number so that the Parliamentary Secretary can check this later. On page 4808 appears this question by Mr. Jolin:
-is it accurate that it is you who have suggested or have insisted with Mr. Lamontagne in order to detail somebody to listen to the conversation, or is it not rather Mr. Lamontagne who asked you to send someone?
A. It is I that called Mr. Lamontagne, having been requested to do so by Inspector Drapeau.
Q. Is it you who have taken the necessary steps in order to have the conversation taped?
A. No. My instructions were to ex-Sergeant Crevier to listen to the conversation on an extension line.
Q. Has anyone to your knowledge taken other necessary steps to have the conversation recorded?
A. The only knowledge that I have of that was that on a previous occasion, on the 11th, I believe, I had sent Sergeant Crevier with specific instructions to record-
It says "record"; I want to underline that.
-a telephone conversation which was presumed to be-which was believed to be in the offing at eight p.m. that evening. The conversation did not take place. Therefore there was no recording made.
At page 4815 appears the following:
Q. Mr. Carriere, do you presently have at your disposal, or did you at that time have, that is to say did you have at your disposal the necessary technical means to tape amongst other things telephone conversations?
A. Yes.
Q. Were at that time the facilities available to you?
A. Yes, there were.
Then at page 4816:
Q. It was possible then. Were the instructions that you received from your superiors to the effect that Mr. Crevier was to listen to the conversation on another line or on another telephone?
A. No, there was a request from Inspector Drapeau to cover a telephone conversation which was going to take place between Raymond Denis and Lawyer Lamontagne.
Q. M. Carriere, does the word "cover", in your mind, simply mean that M. Crevier was to sit beside another telephone and listen to the conversation, or could it not also have meant: tape the ongoing conversation?
A. It could mean either, either to listen or to record it.
At page 4817:
Q. Would not Mr. Carriere have been in a position to instal your equipment the preceding day or during the night?
A. No, that would have been impossible because I was not aware of that coming conversation until that morning, possibly nine-thirty, ten o'clock.
And so on, and so forth, Mr. Speaker.
I point out again that this is an official record of answers given by the Inspector of the R.C.M.P. who worked on the Rivard case, who said at the public hearing before
June 21, 1965
2736	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Mr. Justice Dorion that the R.C.M.P. was preparing to record the conversation which they expected to take place between Mr. Lamontagne and Mr. Rouleau, and that they had the equipment to do it.
I would repeat what I said on other occasions. I am opposed to wire tapping. But surely if it is necessary, and the law enforcement agencies of this country believe it is necessary, then they ought not to hide the fact that it is done. They should not lie to the public or to this House but should ask the Minister to bring in the legislation which is required.

maintopic: EDUCATION-NOVA SCOTIA-REQUEST FOR INCREASED GRANTS TO UNIVERSITIES
EDUCATION-NOVA SCOTIA-REQUEST FOR INCREASED GRANTS TO UNIVERSITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I know it is 20 minutes after ten o'clock but I wish to discuss tonight the problem of the financial emergency facing universities in Canada in general and in particular those in Nova Scotia and the other Maritime Provinces. Under the present federal university grants formula which has been in existence for some years a very great injustice is being done to provinces which, because of the quality of their universities, are able to attract students in great numbers from outside their own provincial borders. I am sure all hon. Members will agree that it is in the interests of Canadian unity and Canadian nationality that our universities should not become strictly provincial in scope and outlook with regard to the area from which they are to draw their students. The present formula,
I contend, forces upon universities and Provincial Governments such an attitude because under the present formula federal grants to universities are based on the population of the province rather than the student population. We find a situation wherein, in Nova Scotia, the amount per student is $183 per year, compared to the universities in Ontario which receive $282 per student per year. So, you see there is a difference of just $99 extra being paid to universities for each student in Ontario as compared to Nova Scotia. Of course, you find these figures vary between the various Provinces. British Columbia is the second worst done by province after Nova Scotia, and they receive only $194 per student per year.
1 suggest that this is an extremely unfair formula and must be revised very quickly.
I am aware that the Bladen Commission is presently investigating the revision of the formula. I am hopeful that they will come forth with some answer that will provide recognition to the provinces which have, through the quality of their universities, been able to attract students from outside their provincial boundaries. I want to say that in the Province of Nova Scotia the problem is twofold. There is not only the question of imported students coming from other areas, but in addition there is the problem of exported graduates. You will find there is a
[Mr. MacEachen.l

sizeable proportion of the student graduates from universities in Nova Scotia going forth to take prominent positions in other parts of this country. We have seen graduates from our universities, who represent other areas in Canada, who have subsequently become Prime Ministers and Premiers of Provinces. I believe there are recent examples. We have seen graduates who have become Cabinet Ministers in other parts of the country, captains of industry and in general men who have played very prominent parts in the life of other provinces. In effect, therefore, the Province of Nova Scotia has been subsidizing other provinces by educating these people and then sending them forth. These are two factors which I think should be given consideration in considering a new formula.
I want to say that while we must wait for the Bladen Commission report, it is a fact that at the moment the Federal Government is spending about one third of 1 per cent of federal expenditures on direct grants to higher education. I believe that just is not good enough. Our universities today have only one controlled source of revenue, and that is tuition fees. If they do not receive greater grants from the federal and provincial governments the only way they can find the money they must have is to put the squeeze upon hard-pressed students, who I think already pay enough to get an education. We in the Maritime Provinces area feel that before the Bladen report comes out the present grants should be upgraded. As you know, they are based on university costs of operating, and operating expenditures for the year 1962.
The previous Government, in fairness I must say, twice upgraded the amount of the grant. I feel that even while the Bladen Commission is investigating the formula it should be changed. There is no reason why the Government could not now, as an interim measure, base the grants on 1965 costs and thus increase the amount. This is in consideration of the fact, we are told by eminent authorities, that there is a 16 per cent annual increase in operating costs of universities in this country.
We in the Maritimes take education very seriously. We consider universities an industry, and they have been an important industry, an industry which is well suited for an area in which it is sometimes difficult to get other types of industry. If we cannot receive from the Federal Government, through these grants in the future an amount that is equal to the assistance that is desperately
June 21, 1965

needed by these universities, then we must think in terms of asking the Atlantic Development Board for such assistance.
It should not be necessary to do this. Nevertheless we might have to think in terms of turning to the Atlantic Development Board to seek assistance in providing the ability for our universities to continue with the fine work they have been doing across the years.
I suggest it is important and crucial in the Maritimes at present, and in Nova Scotia in particular, and that our universities are in desperate need of new funds. I hope the Government will consider this very serious matter.
